 Standardized Nursing Languages (SNL): A common language or terminology used in the nursing profession to ensure that nursing practice, interventions, and outcomes are documented consistently across different facilities
 Primary Nursing: A delivery model of care where one nurse is assigned responsibility for the total care of a specific patient throughout their hospital stay, emphasizing continuity of care and accountability
 Float Pool: A staffing strategy where a group of nurses is not assigned to a permanent unit but instead "floats" to different departments based on daily patient volume and staffing needs
 Acuity System: A method used to determine the intensity of nursing care required by a patient, which directly influences staffing ratios and the distribution of the nursing workload
 Magnet Recognition Program: A status granted by the ANCC to healthcare organizations that demonstrate excellence in nursing leadership, professional practice, and high-quality patient outcomes
 Bioethics: A field of study addressing ethical issues and dilemmas that arise in medicine and biology, providing nurses with a framework for handling complex moral questions such as end-of-life care or genetic testing

title: Pharmacy Exit Exam Comprehensive Revision Note
content:
Pharmacy is the science and technique of preparing, dispensing, and reviewing drugs and providing additional clinical services
 Pharmacist is a healthcare professional who practices in pharmacy
 Pharmacology is the branch of medicine and biology concerned with the study of drug action
 Pharmacokinetics is the study of drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion
 Pharmacodynamics is the study of the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs on the body
 Pharmaceutical care involves the responsible provision of drug therapy for the purpose of achieving definite outcomes that improve patients' quality of life.
Pharmaceutical manufacturing is the process of producing pharmaceutical drugs by industrial scale methods
 Compounding is the creation of a particular pharmaceutical product to fit the unique needs of a patient
 Extemporaneous compounding is the preparation of a pharmaceutical product from scratch according to a prescription or a doctor's order
 Quality control in pharmaceutical manufacturing ensures that drugs are manufactured consistently and meet quality standards
 Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is a system for ensuring that products are consistently produced and controlled according to quality standards.
 Dispensing is the process of preparing and giving out prescribed medications
 Prescription is a written direction from a prescriber to a pharmacist for the compounding, dispensing, and administration of drugs to a patient
 Auxiliary labels provide additional instructions or warnings about how to use a medication
 Pharmaceutical calculations involve mathematical calculations related to medication dosages, dilutions, and compounding
 Pharmaceutical packaging is the process of enclosing pharmaceutical products for distribution, storage, sale, and use
 Institutional formulary is a list of medications approved for use within a healthcare institution.
 Community pharmacy is a pharmacy that deals directly with the public and provides prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and other health-related services
 Hospital pharmacy is a specialized field of pharmacy that focuses on the safe and effective use of medications in a hospital setting
 Clinical pharmacy is a branch of pharmacy where pharmacists provide patient care that optimizes the use of medication and promotes health, wellness, and disease prevention
 Pharmaceutical care is a patient-centered, outcomes-oriented pharmacy practice that requires the pharmacist to work in concert with the patient and the patient's other healthcare providers to promote health, prevent disease, and assess, monitor, initiate, and modify medication use to assure that drug therapy regimens are safe and effective.
Regulatory affairs in pharmacy involves ensuring compliance with laws, regulations, guidelines, and standards related to pharmaceuticals
 Drug scheduling is the classification of drugs into categories based on their potential for abuse, addiction, and medical use
 Drug approval process is the process by which pharmaceutical drugs are approved for sale and marketing by regulatory authorities.
Drug Information: Drug information involves providing accurate and unbiased information about medications to healthcare professionals and patients
 Drug interactions occur when one drug affects the activity of another drug when both are administered together
 Adverse drug reactions (ADR) are unwanted or harmful reactions experienced after the administration of a drug or combination of drugs under normal conditions of use.
Pharmacy Ethics: Pharmacy ethics encompasses the moral principles and values that guide the profession of pharmacy
 Patient confidentiality is the ethical duty of healthcare professionals to protect patient information
 Informed consent is the process by which a healthcare provider ensures that a patient understands the risks and benefits of a medical treatment or procedure before agreeing to it.
Pharmacy Economics:Pharmacy economics involves the financial aspects of pharmacy practice, including pricing, reimbursement, and cost-effectiveness
 Cost-benefit analysis is a method of comparing the costs and benefits of a decision, policy, or program to determine its feasibility or desirability
 Third-party payers are entities other than the patient and healthcare provider that reimburse healthcare expenses, such as insurance companies or government programs.
Pharmacy Management: Pharmacy management involves overseeing the operations of a pharmacy, including staffing, inventory management, and customer service
 Inventory management is the process of efficiently overseeing the constant flow of products into and out of an existing inventory
 Staffing involves recruiting, hiring, training, and managing employees within a pharmacy.
Pharmacy Technology:Pharmacy technology encompasses the tools, equipment, and systems used to support pharmacy operations
 Pharmacy automation refers to the use of technology to streamline and automate pharmacy processes, such as medication dispensing and inventory management
 Electronic health records (EHRs) are digital versions of patients' paper charts that contain their medical history, diagnoses, medications, treatment plans, immunization dates, allergies, radiology images, and laboratory test results.
Pharmacy law encompasses the laws, regulations, and legal principles that govern the practice of pharmacy
 Drug laws regulate the manufacture, distribution, dispensing, and use of medications
 Controlled substances laws regulate the production, distribution, and use of controlled substances
 Patient privacy laws protect patients' rights to privacy and confidentiality regarding their medical information.
Anesthetic – A drug that causes anesthesia. Anesthesia is a short-term and reversible loss of consciousness. Anesthetics are used to perform surgeries without patients having to suffer through the pain
Bactericidal – Drugs that destroy or kill bacteria
Buccal – A process for quick absorption of medication by dissolving a tablet between the cheek and gum
Closed formulary – Drugs not in an approved list. They require prior authorization or may not be covered by the insurer
Chronic – An illness that persists for a long period of time or has frequent recurrence
Diuretic – Drugs that increase the body’s urine discharge flow. This decreases overall fluid accumulation
Dose/dosage – The specified amount and quantity of the drug to be taken at one time
Elixir – A solution that is taken orally and contains one or more active drugs. It is usually alcoholic and sweetened
Generic drug – A medication not protected by patent, distributed and marketed under its pharmaceutical or chemical name, usually by multiple manufacturers at a lower end-user cost
Intracardiac – An injection administered directly into the patient’s heart
Ointment – A preparation of medication disbursed in a thick fluid, typically used to treat skin disorders
Parenteral – Drugs administered directly, and not through the intestinal tract
Placebo – Commonly referred to as a sugar pill. A placebo contains no medicine, but the patient thinks it does, and results may occur because of this belief. Placebos are mostly used in clinical trials to experiment with groups of people in double-blind studies
Syrup – A liquid preparation typically containing a high concentration of sugar (or sugar substitute), a flavoring agent, and active drug ingredients
Transdermal – Administering a drug through the skin, usually with a patch or ointment
Pharmacovigilance: The practice of monitoring the effects of medical drugs after they have been licensed for use, especially in order to identify and evaluate previously unreported adverse reactions
Medication Therapy Management (MTM): A service provided by pharmacists to optimize therapeutic outcomes for patients. Involves comprehensive medication reviews, patient education, and adherence monitoring
Personalized Medicine: Tailoring medical treatment to the individual characteristics of each patient. In pharmacy, this involves pharmacogenomics—studying how genes affect a person's response to drugs—to customize medication therapy
Pharmaceutical Biotechnology: The application of biotechnology principles to develop pharmaceutical products. Involves biopharmaceuticals, genetic engineering, and recombinant DNA technology
Nuclear Pharmacy: Specialized area of pharmacy focusing on the preparation and dispensing of radioactive materials used in diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Involves radiation safety and handling procedures
Medication Adherence: The extent to which patients take medications as prescribed by their healthcare providers. Involves patient education, adherence counseling, and monitoring techniques
Veterinary Pharmacy: Specialty practice focusing on the preparation and dispensing of medications for animals. Involves knowledge of veterinary pharmacology, dosage forms, and regulatory requirements
Pharmaceutical Waste Management: Proper disposal and management of pharmaceutical waste to prevent environmental contamination and ensure public safety. Involves regulations for hazardous waste disposal and sustainability practices 
 Absorption: The process by which a drug enters the bloodstream from the site of administration. 
 Acid-Base Balance: The regulation of pH levels in the body to maintain homeostasis, crucial for drug effectiveness. 
 Adverse Drug Reaction (ADR): Unintended, harmful effects of a drug when administered at normal doses. 
 Agonist: A substance that binds to a receptor and produces a response, often mimicking the action of a natural substance. 
 Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH): An enzyme involved in the metabolism of aldehydes, including those produced during alcohol metabolism. 
 Allergic Reaction: An immune system response to a substance (such as a drug) that the body mistakenly identifies as harmful. 
 Amoxicillin: A commonly prescribed antibiotic used to treat a variety of bacterial infections. 
 Analgesic: A drug used to relieve pain. 
 Anaphylaxis: A severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that requires immediate treatment. 
 Antagonist: A substance that binds to a receptor but does not trigger a response, preventing activation by other molecules. 
 Bioavailability: The proportion of a drug that enters the circulation when administered and is made available to the target tissues. 
 Biosimilar: A biologic medical product highly similar to an already approved reference biologic, with no clinically meaningful differences. 
 Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB): A selective permeability barrier that protects the brain from potentially harmful substances in the blood. 
 Bupropion: An antidepressant and smoking cessation aid, known for its stimulating effects. 
 Beta-Blockers: A class of drugs that reduce blood pressure and heart rate by blocking the effects of adrenaline on beta-adrenergic receptors. 
 Biologic Drugs: Medications derived from living organisms, often used for diseases like cancer or autoimmune disorders. 
 Blood Pressure (BP): The force of circulating blood against the walls of blood vessels, important in determining cardiovascular health. 
 Benzodiazepines: A class of drugs that act as central nervous system depressants, used for anxiety, insomnia, and muscle relaxation. 
 Buffer: A substance that helps to maintain the pH balance of a solution, preventing drastic changes in acidity or alkalinity. 
 Bactericidal: Drugs that kill bacteria, as opposed to bacteriostatic drugs that inhibit bacterial growth. 
 Cytochrome P450: A group of enzymes involved in drug metabolism, affecting the breakdown of medications in the liver. 
 Controlled Substances: Drugs that are regulated by law due to their potential for abuse or addiction. 
 Capsule: A form of oral medication consisting of a gelatin shell that contains the active drug, often in powder or liquid form. 
 Corticosteroids: A class of drugs that reduce inflammation and suppress the immune system, often used for autoimmune diseases and allergies. 
 Chronic Disease: A long-lasting condition that can be controlled but not cured, such as diabetes or hypertension. 
 Clinical Pharmacology: The study of drugs and their clinical use in humans, including their effects, side effects, and optimal use. 
 Chemical Half-Life: The time it takes for the concentration of a drug to decrease by half in the body. 
 Compounding: The process of preparing personalized medications by mixing different ingredients according to a doctor's prescription. 
 Cardiotonic: A drug used to increase the force of heart muscle contraction, commonly used in heart failure. 
 CYP450 Enzymes: A family of enzymes that play a key role in the metabolism of various drugs, influencing their effectiveness and safety. 
 Dosage Form: The physical form in which a drug is produced and administered, such as tablets, capsules, or injections. 
 Dissolution: The process by which a drug dissolves in the body to become available for absorption. 
 Drug Interaction: A situation where one drug affects the activity of another when both are administered together. 
 Dose-Response Relationship: The correlation between the dose of a drug and the magnitude of its effect. 
 Diuretic: A drug that increases the excretion of urine, often used to treat conditions like hypertension and edema. 
 Drug Metabolism: The process by which the body breaks down and converts drugs into active or inactive forms, mainly in the liver. 
 Dosing Schedule: The timing and frequency with which a drug should be administered to achieve optimal therapeutic effects. 
 Drug Tolerance: A condition where the body's response to a drug decreases over time, requiring higher doses to achieve the same effect. 
 Depot Injection: A type of injection designed to release the drug slowly over time, providing long-term treatment. 
 Drug Toxicity: Harmful effects caused by excessive doses of a drug, leading to adverse health consequences. 
 Enzyme Inhibition: A process in which a drug or molecule reduces the activity of an enzyme, often to prevent disease progression. 
 Efficacy: The ability of a drug to produce a desired therapeutic effect when administered at a particular dose. 
 Enteric Coating: A protective layer applied to oral tablets or capsules to prevent them from dissolving in the stomach, ensuring they reach the intestines. 
 Excretion: The process by which the body eliminates waste products and drugs, mainly through the kidneys. 
 Excipients: Inactive substances used in drug formulations to provide bulk or facilitate the absorption of the active ingredient. 
 Endocrine System: A system of glands that secrete hormones, affecting various bodily functions and often targeted by drugs in hormone therapy. 
 Epidemiology: The study of how diseases and medications affect populations, often guiding pharmaceutical research. 
 Erythropoiesis: The process of producing red blood cells, often stimulated by drugs like erythropoietin in anemia treatment. 
 Eosinophils: A type of white blood cell involved in allergic reactions and fighting parasitic infections. 
 Enteral Nutrition: The provision of nutrition through the gastrointestinal tract, often via feeding tubes when oral intake is not possible. 
 Formulation: The process of combining different chemical substances to create a final drug product, including the active ingredients and excipients. 
 First-Pass Metabolism: The initial metabolism of a drug in the liver after oral administration, which can reduce the drug's bioavailability. 
 Fentanyl: A potent synthetic opioid analgesic used to treat severe pain, often in cancer patients or post-surgery. 
 Free Drug: The portion of a drug that is not bound to proteins in the blood and is available to produce its effects. 
 FDA (Food and Drug Administration): The U.S. government agency responsible for regulating food, drugs, and medical devices to ensure safety and effectiveness. 
 Furosemide: A diuretic used to treat conditions like hypertension and edema by increasing urine production and reducing fluid retention. 
 Pharmacovigilance: The practice of monitoring the safety and effectiveness of medications after they have been released to the market. 
 Pharmacokinetics: The study of how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolizes, and excretes drugs. 
 Fusion Protein: A genetically engineered protein that combines two different proteins, often used for targeted therapies. 
 Food-Drug Interaction: The influence that food may have on the absorption, metabolism, or elimination of drugs, altering their effectiveness. 
 Gene Therapy: A medical treatment that involves altering or replacing defective genes in the body to treat genetic disorders. 
 Gastrointestinal (GI) Tract: The organ system involved in the ingestion and digestion of food, often impacted by drugs administered orally. 
 Generic Drug: A drug that is equivalent to a brand-name drug in terms of dosage, strength, and therapeutic effect, but is typically less expensive. 
 Glucocorticoids: A type of corticosteroid hormone used in treating inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. 
 Glucose Metabolism: The process by which the body breaks down glucose for energy, influenced by drugs used in treating diabetes. 
 GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid): A neurotransmitter that inhibits neural activity, often targeted by medications for anxiety or epilepsy. 
 Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor (G-CSF): A drug that stimulates the production of white blood cells, particularly neutrophils, to help fight infections. 
 Gastroprotective Agents: Drugs used to protect the gastrointestinal lining from damage caused by NSAIDs, alcohol, or infections. 
 Glycosuria: The presence of glucose in the urine, typically indicative of diabetes or other metabolic disorders. 
 Gastric Emptying: The process by which food and liquids leave the stomach and enter the small intestine, which can be influenced by certain medications. 
 Hepatic Metabolism: The breakdown of drugs in the liver, which is essential for the detoxification and activation of certain medications. 
 Hematopoiesis: The process of blood cell formation, stimulated by growth factors and certain drugs. 
 Hypertension: High blood pressure, a common condition treated with antihypertensive drugs like ACE inhibitors, diuretics, and beta-blockers. 
 Histamine: A compound involved in immune responses and allergic reactions, often blocked by antihistamines in conditions like hay fever. 
 Half-Life: The time required for the concentration of a drug in the blood to decrease by half, a key parameter in determining dosing schedules. 
 Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT): The use of medications to replace hormones that the body no longer produces, commonly used in menopausal women. 
 Hepatotoxicity: Toxicity or damage to the liver caused by drugs or chemicals, which can result in liver failure if severe. 
 High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC): A laboratory technique used to separate and quantify compounds in a drug formulation. 
 Hyperglycemia: Elevated blood glucose levels, often treated with insulin or other medications in patients with diabetes. 
 Hyperkalemia: Elevated potassium levels in the blood, a potential side effect of certain drugs, such as ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics. 
 Immunosuppressants: Drugs that reduce or suppress the immune system's activity, commonly used in organ transplant patients to prevent rejection. 
 Intravenous (IV) Administration: The delivery of a drug directly into the bloodstream through a vein, providing immediate effects. 
 Insulin: A hormone used to regulate blood glucose levels, primarily used in the treatment of type 1 and type 2 diabetes. 
 Inhalers: Devices used to deliver medications directly into the lungs for respiratory conditions, such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). 
 Iatrogenic Disease: A condition that is caused by medical treatment or diagnostic procedures, often related to drug side effects. 
 Indications: The medical conditions or diseases for which a drug is approved and recommended for use. 
 Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: A class of cancer immunotherapy drugs that enhance the immune system's ability to target and destroy cancer cells. 
 Inotropic Drugs: Medications that alter the force of heart contractions, used in conditions like heart failure. 
 Isomer: Compounds with the same chemical formula but different structures, which may lead to differences in drug activity and side effects. 
 Infection Control: The practice of preventing and managing infections, particularly in hospitals, using medications like antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals. 
 Jaundice: A condition characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes, often associated with liver disease or drug-induced liver injury. 
 J-Codes: Codes used to identify drugs and biologicals administered in outpatient settings, primarily in the United States. 
 Joint Pain: A common side effect of many medications, including certain statins, steroids, and biologic agents. 
 Jitter: Variations in the timing of drug delivery or response, often observed in electronic drug delivery systems. 
 Junctional Tachycardia: A type of arrhythmia originating from the atrioventricular junction, often treated with antiarrhythmic drugs. 
 J-Drug: A designation for certain drugs used in outpatient settings, particularly under Medicare Part B. 
 Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): The pressure in the jugular vein, often used as a clinical indicator of fluid status or heart failure. 
 Jargon: The specialized terminology used in the pharmaceutical industry to describe processes, procedures, and substances. 
 Jet Lag: A temporary sleep disorder caused by traveling across time zones, sometimes treated with melatonin or other sleep aids. 
 Junctional Rhythm: A type of heart rhythm originating in the AV junction, sometimes associated with abnormal drug effects 
 Ketosis: A metabolic state in which the body burns fat for fuel instead of carbohydrates, sometimes used in ketogenic diets or induced by medications for weight loss. 
 Kidney Function: Refers to the performance of the kidneys in filtering blood and excreting waste, which can be affected by various medications. 
 Keratoconjunctivitis: Inflammation of the cornea and conjunctiva, sometimes caused by drug reactions or certain medications. 
 Kinetics: The study of the movement of drugs within the body, including absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. 
 Kaliuresis: The excretion of potassium in the urine, often increased by certain diuretics or other medications. 
 Kinin: A class of peptides involved in inflammation and vasodilation, which may be targeted by certain drugs to manage pain or inflammation. 
 Ketoacidosis: A dangerous condition where the body produces high levels of ketones, often in diabetic patients or those undergoing starvation. 
 Knee Arthroplasty: A surgical procedure to replace a knee joint, often requiring postoperative medication management, including pain control. 
 Karyotype: A laboratory technique used to examine the number and structure of chromosomes, often in genetic disorders. 
 Kinetochore: A structure on chromosomes involved in cell division, which may be targeted in cancer treatments. 
 Lipid Metabolism: The biochemical process by which the body breaks down fats and uses them for energy, often influenced by drugs like statins. 
 Liver Enzymes: Proteins produced by the liver that help metabolize drugs; altered liver enzyme levels may affect drug metabolism. 
 Lactation: The process of milk production in mammals, influenced by hormones and sometimes impacted by drugs that a mother may take. 
 Laparotomy: A surgical procedure involving an incision into the abdominal cavity, sometimes requiring medication for post-operative pain management. 
 Leukemia: A type of cancer affecting blood cells, often treated with chemotherapy drugs or targeted therapies. 
 Lymphoma: A cancer of the lymphatic system, treated with chemotherapy, radiation, and immunotherapy drugs. 
 Lysosomal Storage Diseases: A group of inherited metabolic disorders that result from defects in lysosomal function, often requiring specialized drug therapy. 
 Lactose Intolerance: The inability to digest lactose due to a lack of the enzyme lactase, which may require dietary modifications or enzyme supplements. 
 Liposomes: Tiny spherical vesicles used as drug delivery systems, allowing for targeted delivery of medications. 
 Long-Acting Medications: Drugs formulated to release slowly over time, providing sustained effects with less frequent dosing. 
 Metabolism: The process by which the body converts drugs into metabolites, impacting the drug's activity and duration of effect. 
 Migraine: A type of headache that can be managed with various medications, including pain relievers and triptans. 
 Myocardial Infarction (MI): A heart attack, often treated with drugs such as thrombolytics, anticoagulants, and beta-blockers. 
 Mitochondrial Diseases: Disorders caused by dysfunction in mitochondria, often requiring medications that address cellular energy production. 
 Molecular Pharmacology: The study of drug interactions at the molecular level, particularly how drugs bind to their receptors and exert their effects. 
 Metoclopramide: A medication used to treat nausea, vomiting, and gastroparesis by enhancing gastric motility. 
 Monoclonal Antibodies: Laboratory-made molecules that act as substitutes for the immune system's antibodies, used in treating cancers and autoimmune diseases. 
 Medicare Part D: A part of the U.S. Medicare program that provides prescription drug coverage. 
 Methylxanthines: A class of drugs that includes caffeine, theophylline, and theobromine, which have stimulant effects on the central nervous system. 
 Mast Cell Stabilizers: Medications that prevent the release of histamine and other chemicals from mast cells, used in managing allergic reactions and asthma. 
 Neurotransmitters: Chemical messengers that transmit signals across synapses in the brain, often targeted by psychiatric and neurological medications. 
 Narcotics: A class of drugs that include opioids, used for pain relief but also associated with a high potential for addiction and misuse. 
 NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs): A group of drugs used to reduce inflammation, pain, and fever, such as ibuprofen and aspirin. 
 N-acetylcysteine: A medication used to treat acetaminophen overdose and chronic respiratory conditions, acting as a mucolytic agent. 
 Nutraceuticals: Foods or food products that provide health benefits beyond basic nutrition, sometimes used in conjunction with pharmaceutical therapies. 
 Nausea: A feeling of unease or discomfort in the stomach, often treated with antiemetic medications. 
 Nephrotoxicity: Kidney toxicity caused by drugs or chemicals, which may result in kidney damage or failure. 
 Nicotinic Receptors: A type of receptor involved in neurotransmission, targeted by drugs like nicotine or certain medications for neurological conditions. 
 Nutrient Interactions: The effects of food, vitamins, or minerals on the absorption or effectiveness of drugs. 
 Nucleoside Analogs: Synthetic drugs that mimic nucleotides, used in the treatment of viral infections and some cancers. 
 Opioids: A class of drugs used to relieve pain by acting on the central nervous system. Examples include morphine, oxycodone, and fentanyl. 
 Oncology: The branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, often involving chemotherapeutic and immunological drug therapies. 
 Osmosis: The movement of solvent molecules from an area of lower solute concentration to an area of higher solute concentration, which can influence drug absorption and distribution. 
 Oral Administration: The method of taking medication through the mouth in the form of tablets, capsules, or liquids. 
 Opiate Antagonists: Drugs that block the effects of opioids, such as naloxone, used in treating opioid overdose. 
 Ophthalmic Drugs: Medications formulated for use in the eye to treat conditions such as glaucoma, dry eyes, or infections. 
 Over-the-Counter (OTC): Drugs available without a prescription, typically for treating common, less severe health conditions. 
 Onset of Action: The time it takes for a drug to begin to produce its therapeutic effects after administration. 
 Ototoxicity: Damage to the ear, particularly the cochlea or auditory nerve, as a result of drug use, often caused by certain antibiotics or chemotherapy drugs. 
 Orthostatic Hypotension: A sudden drop in blood pressure when standing up, which can be a side effect of medications like antihypertensives. 
 Pharmacokinetics: The study of how drugs are absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted by the body. 
 Pharmacodynamics: The study of the effects of drugs on the body, including how they interact with receptors and produce therapeutic effects. 
 Pharmaceutical Care: The practice of providing patient-centered care to optimize drug therapy, improve outcomes, and minimize adverse effects. 
 Pharmacogenomics: The study of how an individual's genetic makeup affects their response to drugs, allowing for personalized medicine. 
 Placebo: An inert substance given as a control in clinical trials, or used in some cases to provide psychological benefits to patients. 
 Polypharmacy: The use of multiple medications by a patient, which can increase the risk of drug interactions and side effects. 
 Pharmacovigilance: The monitoring of the safety of pharmaceutical products, especially in terms of identifying and reporting adverse drug reactions. 
 Parenteral Administration: Delivery of drugs by injection or infusion, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract (e.g., intravenous, intramuscular). 
 Pharmaceutics: The science of preparing and dispensing medications, including drug formulation and design. 
 Psychoactive Drugs: Substances that affect the mind, mood, or behavior, including antidepressants, antipsychotics, and recreational drugs. 
 Quality Control (QC): The process of ensuring that pharmaceutical products meet required standards of quality, purity, and potency. 
 Quinine: A drug used to treat malaria, derived from the bark of the cinchona tree. 
 Quantum Medicine: A branch of alternative medicine that applies principles of quantum mechanics to understand drug effects at the molecular and submolecular levels. 
 Quantitative Analysis: The measurement of the quantity of drug in a given sample, typically performed in pharmaceutical research and production. 
 Quinolones: A class of broad-spectrum antibiotics used to treat bacterial infections, such as ciprofloxacin. 
 Quality Assurance (QA): The procedures and policies implemented to ensure that drugs are manufactured and delivered in accordance with regulatory standards. 
 Quenching: The process of stopping or slowing down a chemical reaction, such as in the production of certain pharmaceutical products. 
 QRS Complex: A part of the electrocardiogram (ECG) that represents the electrical activity of the ventricles; some drugs can influence its duration. 
 Quantification: The process of determining the concentration or amount of a substance in a sample. 
 Quorum Sensing: A process in bacterial communities that involves the regulation of gene expression in response to population density; certain antibiotics target this mechanism. 
 Receptor: A protein on the surface of or within a cell that binds to specific substances (e.g., drugs or hormones) to trigger a cellular response. 
 Resistance: The ability of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses) to withstand the effects of a drug, especially antibiotics. 
 Rheumatoid Arthritis: An autoimmune disorder treated with immunosuppressive drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), or biologics. 
 Reverse Transcription: A process by which RNA is converted into DNA, targeted by certain antiretroviral drugs in the treatment of HIV. 
 Renal Toxicity: Kidney damage caused by medications, which can lead to kidney failure and requires careful drug monitoring. 
 Rebound Effect: A phenomenon in which symptoms worsen after discontinuing a medication, commonly seen with corticosteroids or certain antihypertensives. 
 Radiopharmaceuticals: Drugs that contain radioactive substances used in diagnostic imaging or cancer treatment. 
 Resting Potential: The electrical charge difference across a cell membrane at rest, influenced by ion channels that are targeted by certain drugs. 
 Rash: A common adverse effect of many drugs, such as antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and chemotherapies. 
 Rapid-Acting Insulin: A type of insulin with a quick onset of action used to control blood glucose levels, particularly for meal-time insulin needs. 
 Side Effects: Unintended or adverse effects that occur in addition to the therapeutic effect of a drug. 
 Sublingual Administration: The process of placing a drug under the tongue for absorption, allowing it to enter the bloodstream rapidly. 
 Statins: A class of drugs used to lower cholesterol levels by inhibiting the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. 
 Steroids: A class of drugs that mimic the effects of hormones like cortisol, used in treating inflammation, autoimmune diseases, and some cancers. 
 Synergy: The interaction between two or more drugs that results in a greater effect than the sum of their individual effects. 
 Serotonin: A neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation, targeted by antidepressants such as SSRIs and SNRIs. 
 Sodium Channel Blockers: Drugs that inhibit the movement of sodium ions across cell membranes, commonly used in antiarrhythmic therapy. 
 Stimulants: Drugs that increase activity in the central nervous system, used to treat conditions like ADHD or narcolepsy. 
 Sustained-Release: Medications formulated to release their active ingredient gradually over time, reducing the frequency of dosing. 
 Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs): A class of antidepressants that block the reuptake of serotonin in the brain to improve mood. 
 Toxicology: The study of the harmful effects of substances, including drugs, on the body. 
 Therapeutic Index: The ratio between the toxic dose and the effective dose of a drug; a higher index indicates a safer drug. 
 Transdermal: A method of drug administration through the skin using patches that allow drugs to be absorbed slowly over time. 
 Titration: The process of gradually adjusting the dose of a drug to find the most effective dose with minimal side effects. 
 Thrombosis: The formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel, which can be treated with anticoagulant medications. 
 Toxic Dose: The amount of a drug that causes toxicity, potentially leading to adverse effects or poisoning. 
 Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM): The measurement of drug concentrations in the blood to ensure they remain within a therapeutic range. 
 Topical Administration: The application of drugs directly to the skin or mucous membranes, such as creams, ointments, or patches. 
 Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs): A class of antidepressants that block the reuptake of neurotransmitters like serotonin and norepinephrine. 
 Thyroid Medications: Drugs used to treat thyroid conditions, such as hypothyroidism, including levothyroxine. 
 Uptake: The process by which cells absorb drugs or other substances from the bloodstream. 
 Ulcerative Colitis: An inflammatory bowel disease that is treated with immunosuppressive drugs, biologics, or corticosteroids. 
 Urinary Tract Infection (UTI): A common bacterial infection treated with antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin or nitrofurantoin. 
 Urease Inhibitors: Drugs used to treat Helicobacter pylori infections, often in combination with antibiotics for peptic ulcers. 
 Unbound Drug: The fraction of a drug in the bloodstream that is not bound to proteins and is pharmacologically active. 
 Urolithiasis: The formation of stones in the urinary tract, which may require surgical intervention or medications to dissolve the stones. 
 Uptake Inhibitors: Drugs that prevent the reabsorption of specific substances, such as serotonin or dopamine, to treat psychiatric conditions. 
 Urine Alkalinizers: Medications used to increase the pH of urine, helping in the treatment of certain conditions like uric acid stones. 
 Urethane: A chemical compound used in the synthesis of various medications, including some anticancer agents. 
 Ursodiol: A bile acid used to treat gallstones and certain liver conditions, such as primary biliary cirrhosis. 
 Vasodilators: Drugs that relax and widen blood vessels, helping to reduce blood pressure and improve blood flow. 
 Vitamins: Essential organic compounds required in small amounts for normal metabolic function; deficiencies can be treated with supplements. 
 Viral Infections: Infections caused by viruses, often treated with antiviral drugs such as acyclovir or antiretrovirals for HIV. 
 Vagus Nerve: A key nerve involved in autonomic functions, which can be targeted by drugs to treat conditions like epilepsy or arrhythmias. 
 Vasopressors: Medications that constrict blood vessels and raise blood pressure, used in conditions like shock or severe hypotension. 
 Ventricular Arrhythmia: Abnormal heart rhythms originating in the ventricles, treated with antiarrhythmic medications like amiodarone. 
 Vaginal Suppositories: A dosage form of medication inserted into the vagina for local treatment, often for infections or hormonal therapy. 
 Viral Load: The amount of virus present in the bloodstream, particularly in HIV or hepatitis, which is monitored to gauge treatment effectiveness. 
 Viral Hepatitis: Liver inflammation caused by viral infections such as hepatitis B and C, often treated with antiviral medications. 
 Vaccine: A biological preparation that provides active acquired immunity to a particular infectious disease. 
 Warfarin: A blood thinner used to prevent blood clots in conditions such as atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism. 
 WBC (White Blood Cells): Cells in the blood that are part of the immune system; their count is often monitored in response to infections or chemotherapy. 
 Wound Healing: The process of tissue repair, which can be enhanced with drugs such as antibiotics or corticosteroids to prevent infection and inflammation. 
 Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome: A neurological disorder caused by thiamine deficiency, often seen in chronic alcoholics; treated with thiamine supplements. 
 White Blood Cell Count: The number of white blood cells in the blood, which is used to assess immune function and detect infections or blood disorders. 
 Worm Infestations: Infections caused by parasitic worms, which are treated with antiparasitic drugs such as mebendazole or albendazole. 
 Withdrawal Symptoms: The physical and psychological effects experienced when discontinuing certain drugs, such as opioids or alcohol. 
 Whole Blood Transfusion: The process of transfusing a patient with all components of blood, including red blood cells, plasma, and platelets. 
 Wound Infection: An infection in a wound site, often treated with topical or systemic antibiotics to prevent complications. 
 Wound Dressings: Materials applied to a wound to promote healing, absorb exudates, and protect from infection. 
 Xenobiotics: Foreign substances, including drugs and environmental toxins, that enter the body and may have beneficial or harmful effects. 
 X-rays: A type of radiation used for diagnostic imaging, where certain drugs may be used to enhance imaging (e.g., contrast agents). 
 Xenotransplantation: The transplantation of organs or tissues from one species to another, sometimes requiring immunosuppressive drugs. 
 Xenon: A noble gas used in some medical imaging technologies, as well as in anesthetic mixtures. 
 Xenobiotic Metabolism: The process by which the body metabolizes foreign substances, such as drugs, through enzymatic reactions. 
 Xylitol: A sugar alcohol used as a sweetener, which may have medical applications in certain formulations, such as dental products. 
 Xenograft: A tissue or organ transplant from a donor of a different species, often used in research or organ transplantation. 
 Xenogenesis: The production of offspring by individuals of different species, relevant in biotechnology for producing transgenic animals. 
 Xenogenic Infection: An infection caused by a foreign organism, such as a virus or bacteria from another species. 
 Xenon Gas: Used as a contrast agent in imaging studies and sometimes as an anesthetic. 
 Yellow Fever: A viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes, preventable by vaccination, and treated with supportive care. 
 Yersinia: A genus of bacteria that includes pathogens responsible for diseases like the plague, which may require antibiotics for treatment. 
 Yogurt-Based Probiotics: Probiotic products made from yogurt, used to restore gut flora and support gastrointestinal health. 
 Yohimbine: A compound derived from the yohimbe tree, used in some treatments for erectile dysfunction or weight loss, but with significant side effects. 
 Yttrium-90: A radioactive isotope used in cancer treatment, particularly for liver cancer, as part of radioembolization therapy. 
 Yellowing of Skin: A sign of liver dysfunction or jaundice, which may require drugs for treatment or management of liver disease. 
 Yttrium-Based Radiopharmaceuticals: Drugs containing yttrium used in treating cancer by delivering targeted radiation therapy. 
 Yeast Infection: A fungal infection, often caused by Candida species, treated with antifungal medications like fluconazole. 
 Yohimbine Hydrochloride: A medication used to treat erectile dysfunction and for weight loss by increasing fat metabolism. 
 Yogurt as a Prebiotic: Consumed to improve gut health, yogurt contains beneficial bacteria that act as probiotics in the digestive system. 
 Zinc: An essential trace element important for immune function, wound healing, and cell division; used in supplements and certain medications. 
 Zolpidem: A medication used to treat insomnia by affecting GABA receptors in the brain. 
 Zinc Oxide: A compound used in topical ointments and creams, especially for skin protection and wound healing. 
 Zygote: The fertilized egg resulting from the union of sperm and egg; relevant in pharmacology for drugs affecting pregnancy. 
 Zidovudine: An antiretroviral drug used to treat HIV/AIDS by inhibiting reverse transcriptase. 
 Zoonosis: A disease that can be transmitted from animals to humans, which may require antimicrobial or antiparasitic drugs. 
 Zanamivir: An antiviral drug used to treat influenza by inhibiting the viral neuraminidase enzyme. 
 Zepatier: A combination antiviral drug used in the treatment of chronic hepatitis C infections. 
 Zoster Vaccine: A vaccine that prevents shingles, a painful rash caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. 
 Zolmitriptan: A medication used to treat migraine headaches by constricting blood vessels in the brain.
Steady State: The condition in which the rate of drug administration equals the rate of drug elimination, typically reached after 4 to 5 half-lives of regular dosing
Prodrug: A pharmacologically inactive compound that is converted into an active drug through metabolic processes in the body, used to improve bioavailability or reduce toxicity
Volume of Distribution ($V_d$): A theoretical volume that relates the amount of drug in the body to the concentration of drug in the plasma, indicating the extent to which a drug distributes into extravascular tissues
Clearance ($Cl$): The volume of plasma from which a drug is completely removed per unit of time, representing the efficiency of drug elimination by the kidneys or liver
Therapeutic Window: The range of drug dosages or plasma concentrations which can treat disease effectively without having toxic effects; the area between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration
Michaelis-Menten Kinetics: A model of enzyme kinetics that describes how the rate of reaction depends on the concentration of the substrate, critical for understanding "saturation kinetics" where elimination becomes zero-order at high doses
Pharmacophore: The specific ensemble of steric and electronic features that is necessary to ensure the optimal supramolecular interactions with a specific biological target and to trigger its biological response
Enantiomers: Pairs of molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other; in pharmacy, different enantiomers of the same drug can have vastly different therapeutic or toxic effects
Half-life ($t_{1/2}$): The time required for the amount or concentration of a drug in the body to decrease by exactly one-half, used to determine dosing intervals
Loading Dose: An initial higher dose of a drug given at the beginning of a treatment to reach the therapeutic steady-state concentration in the plasma more rapidly
Maintenance Dose: The regular dose of a drug required to maintain the desired therapeutic concentration at steady state by replacing the amount of drug eliminated between doses
Alligation Method: A mathematical technique used in pharmacy to calculate the proportions of two or more substances of different strengths needed to create a mixture of a desired intermediate strength
Isotonicity (E-value): The sodium chloride equivalent of a drug, representing the amount of NaCl that produces the same osmotic effect as 1 gram of the drug, used to adjust the osmotic pressure of ophthalmic and parenteral solutions
Thixotropy: A rheological property of certain pharmaceutical gels or fluids that become less viscous (flow more easily) when shaken and return to a gel-like state when left undisturbed, preventing sedimentation in suspensions
Noyes-Whitney Equation: A mathematical formula that describes the rate of dissolution of solid particles in a liquid, identifying factors like surface area and concentration gradient that influence drug absorption rates
Cellulose Acetate Phthalate (CAP): A common polymer used for enteric coating that remains insoluble at acidic stomach pH but dissolves at the higher pH of the small intestine to protect acid-labile drugs
P-glycoprotein (P-gp): An ATP-dependent efflux pump located in cell membranes that actively transports drugs out of cells (like the brain or gut), often acting as a major mechanism for multi-drug resistance and limited drug absorption
Potency vs. Efficacy: Potency refers to the concentration of drug required to produce a specific effect (position on the x-axis), while efficacy refers to the maximum effect a drug can produce regardless of dose (height on the y-axis)
Idiosyncratic Reaction: An unpredictable and abnormal response to a drug that is not dose-related and occurs in a small number of patients, often due to underlying genetic differences or metabolic abnormalities
Incompatibility: A physical or chemical interaction between two or more ingredients that leads to an undesirable product, such as precipitation, color change, or loss of therapeutic activity when drugs are mixed in the same syringe or IV bag

title: Water Resource Engineering Exit Exam Comprehensive Revision Note
content:
Hydrology: The science dealing with the occurrence, circulation, distribution, and properties of water on, in, and above the Earth's surface, including the hydrologic cycle
Hydrologic Cycle: The continuous circulation of water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff, and groundwater flow
Precipitation: Water released from the atmosphere in liquid or solid form (rain, snow, hail, sleet) that reaches the earth's surface
Evaporation: The process by which liquid water is converted to water vapor and transferred to the atmosphere from open water or soil surfaces
Transpiration: The process by which water absorbed by plant roots is released into the atmosphere as vapor through leaf stomata
Evapotranspiration: The combined loss of water from a land area through evaporation from soil/water surfaces and transpiration from plants
Infiltration: The process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil
Percolation: The downward movement of water through soil layers below the root zone toward the water table
Runoff: That portion of precipitation that flows over the land surface and eventually reaches a stream channel
Interception: Rainfall captured and temporarily stored on vegetation surfaces, part of which evaporates without reaching the ground
Catchment Area (Watershed): The total area that drains to a particular point in a stream or river
Time of Concentration: The time required for runoff to travel from the most hydraulically distant point in a watershed to the outlet
Rational Method: A method for estimating peak runoff using Q=CiA, where C is runoff coefficient, i is rainfall intensity, A is area
Runoff Coefficient: A dimensionless factor representing the fraction of rainfall that becomes surface runoff
SCS Curve Number Method: An empirical method developed by the Soil Conservation Service to estimate direct runoff from rainfall based on land use, soil type, and antecedent moisture
Unit Hydrograph: The hydrograph of direct runoff resulting from one unit of effective rainfall occurring uniformly over a basin in a unit time
Hydrograph: A graph showing the variation of discharge with time at a particular point in a river or channel
Baseflow: The sustained portion of streamflow contributed by groundwater discharge into a stream channel
Recession Curve: The declining limb of a hydrograph following the peak, representing depletion of channel and groundwater storage
Time to Peak: The time interval from the start of rainfall (or rise of hydrograph) to the occurrence of peak discharge
Flood Frequency Analysis: Statistical analysis of historical flood data to estimate the probability of occurrence of floods of various magnitudes
Return Period (Recurrence Interval): The average interval of time within which a given event is expected to be equaled or exceeded at least once
Log-Pearson Type III Distribution: A statistical distribution commonly used in flood frequency analysis to accommodate the skewness typical of flood data
IDF Curve (Intensity-Duration-Frequency): A curve relating rainfall intensity, duration, and return period, used for design storm development
Design Storm: A hypothetical rainfall event with specified intensity, duration, and return period used as design input for hydraulic structures
Alternating Block Method: A method for constructing a design storm hyetograph from IDF curve data
Isohyetal Method: A method of estimating average rainfall over an area using contour lines connecting points of equal rainfall
Thiessen Polygon Method: A method of estimating average rainfall by assigning weighted areas of influence to each rain gauge
Normal Ratio Method: A method for estimating missing rainfall data using nearby station records weighted by normal annual precipitation
Double Mass Curve: A graphical method used to check the consistency of rainfall records over time
Flood Routing: The technique of determining the timing and magnitude of a flood wave as it moves through a river reach or reservoir
Muskingum Method: A hydrologic flood routing method using a storage-discharge relationship with parameters K and X
Kinematic Wave Approximation: A simplified flood routing method that neglects inertial and pressure gradient terms in the momentum equation
Reservoir Routing: The process of determining outflow hydrograph from a reservoir given the inflow hydrograph and storage characteristics
Continuity Equation: The principle of conservation of mass applied to fluid flow, expressed as Q=A1V1=A2V2 for incompressible steady flow
Bernoulli's Equation: An energy conservation equation for fluid flow stating P/γ + V²/2g + z = constant along a streamline
Darcy-Weisbach Equation: An equation for calculating friction head loss in pipe flow, hf=f(L/D)(V²/2g)
Hazen-Williams Equation: An empirical formula for calculating friction head loss in water pipes based on a roughness coefficient C
Manning's Equation: A formula for calculating flow velocity in open channels, V=(1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2)
Chezy's Formula: An open channel flow formula, V=C√(RS), predecessor to Manning's equation
Reynolds Number: A dimensionless number comparing inertial to viscous forces, used to classify flow as laminar or turbulent
Froude Number: A dimensionless number comparing inertial to gravitational forces, used to classify open channel flow as subcritical or supercritical
Laminar Flow: Smooth, orderly fluid motion in parallel layers, occurring at low Reynolds numbers
Turbulent Flow: Chaotic, irregular fluid motion occurring at high Reynolds numbers
Critical Depth: The depth of flow at which specific energy is minimum for a given discharge
Specific Energy: The energy per unit weight of flowing water measured relative to the channel bed, E=y+V²/2g
Alternate Depths: The two depths (subcritical and supercritical) that share the same specific energy value for a given discharge
Hydraulic Jump: An abrupt transition from supercritical to subcritical flow accompanied by significant energy dissipation
Hydraulic Radius: The ratio of flow cross-sectional area to wetted perimeter, R=A/P
Wetted Perimeter: The length of the channel boundary in contact with flowing water
Most Economical Channel Section: A channel cross-section that minimizes wetted perimeter for a given area, maximizing hydraulic efficiency
Weir: A barrier across a channel used to measure flow rate or control upstream water level
Coefficient of Discharge (Cd): An empirical correction factor accounting for energy losses and contraction in flow measurement devices
Venturi Meter: A flow measurement device that uses a constriction in a pipe to create a pressure differential related to flow rate
Orifice: A small opening through which fluid flows, with discharge given by Q=Cd×A×√(2gh)
Torricelli's Theorem: A theorem stating the theoretical velocity of efflux through an orifice equals √(2gh)
Pitot Tube: A device used to measure local fluid velocity by measuring stagnation pressure
Notch: A weir with a specific opening shape (rectangular, triangular/V-notch, trapezoidal) used for precise flow measurement
Backwater Curve: The water surface profile resulting from an obstruction causing flow depth to increase upstream
Gradually Varied Flow: Open channel flow in which depth changes gradually along the channel length
Rapidly Varied Flow: Open channel flow in which depth changes abruptly over a short distance, such as at a hydraulic jump
Specific Discharge (Darcy Flux): The apparent velocity of groundwater flow calculated using the full cross-sectional area, q=Q/A
Seepage Velocity: The actual average velocity of water through pore spaces in an aquifer, v=q/n (n=effective porosity)
Darcy's Law: A law describing groundwater flow through porous media, Q=-KA(dh/dl)
Hydraulic Conductivity (K): A measure of a soil/rock's ability to transmit water under a hydraulic gradient
Transmissivity (T): The rate at which water moves through the full saturated thickness of an aquifer, T=Kb
Storativity (Storage Coefficient, S): The volume of water released from storage per unit area per unit decline in head in a confined aquifer
Specific Yield: The volume of water released from storage per unit area per unit decline in water table in an unconfined aquifer
Specific Retention: The water held in soil pores against gravity drainage, complementary to specific yield (Porosity=Specific Yield+Specific Retention)
Porosity: The ratio of void space to total volume of a soil or rock material
Effective Porosity: The portion of total porosity consisting of interconnected pores through which water can actually flow
Confined Aquifer: An aquifer bounded above and below by impermeable layers, water under pressure
Unconfined Aquifer: An aquifer with a water table as its upper boundary, directly connected to the atmosphere
Aquitard: A geological layer with low but non-zero permeability that retards but does not completely prevent water movement
Aquiclude: An essentially impermeable geological layer that prevents significant water movement
Aquifer Anisotropy: The directional dependence of hydraulic conductivity within an aquifer
Cone of Depression: The radially symmetric depression in the water table or potentiometric surface around a pumping well
Theis Equation: The non-equilibrium equation describing transient drawdown in a confined aquifer due to pumping
Cooper-Jacob Method: A simplified approximation of the Theis equation used to analyze pumping test drawdown data
Pumping Test (Aquifer Test): A controlled field test to determine aquifer hydraulic properties (T and S) by measuring drawdown response
Specific Capacity: The discharge rate per unit drawdown of a well, an indicator of well performance
Safe Yield (Sustainable Yield): The maximum rate of groundwater withdrawal sustainable without long-term depletion or adverse effects
Groundwater Mining: Extraction of groundwater exceeding the natural recharge rate, depleting aquifer storage
Land Subsidence: Gradual sinking of land surface caused by compaction of aquifer materials from excessive groundwater extraction
Ghyben-Herzberg Relationship: An equation estimating the depth of the freshwater-saltwater interface below sea level in coastal aquifers
Saltwater Intrusion: The landward migration of saline water into a freshwater aquifer, often due to excessive pumping
Conjunctive Use: The coordinated management of surface water and groundwater resources together
Recharge: The process by which water enters and replenishes an aquifer, naturally or artificially
Tracer Test: A groundwater investigation method using injected substances to determine flow paths and travel times
Isotope Hydrology: The use of stable or radioactive isotopes as natural tracers in water resources investigations
Dam: A barrier constructed to impound water for storage, flood control, irrigation, or power generation
Gravity Dam: A dam that resists water pressure primarily through its own weight
Arch Dam: A dam that transfers water load horizontally into canyon abutments through arch action
Buttress Dam: A dam supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side
Embankment (Earth) Dam: A dam constructed of compacted soil or rock fill materials
Spillway: A structure designed to safely release excess reservoir water during floods
Ogee Spillway: A curved-profile spillway crest shaped to match the natural underside of a free-falling water jet
Siphon Spillway: A spillway that automatically discharges excess water using siphonic action
Energy Dissipator (Stilling Basin): A structure designed to dissipate the high kinetic energy of spillway discharge, typically via a hydraulic jump
Freeboard: The vertical distance between maximum water level and the top of a dam, levee, or channel
Probable Maximum Flood (PMF): The most extreme flood reasonably possible based on the most severe combination of meteorological conditions
Design Flood: The flood used as the basis for normal hydraulic design of a structure
Check Flood: A larger flood used to verify the structural safety of a dam beyond the design flood
Piping (Internal Erosion): Progressive erosion of seepage paths through an embankment dam or foundation, a major dam failure mechanism
Reservoir Mass Curve (Rippl Diagram): A graphical method plotting cumulative inflow versus time used to determine required reservoir storage capacity
Firm Yield (Safe Yield of Reservoir): The maximum quantity of water reliably suppliable from a reservoir during the most critical drought period
Gross Storage Capacity: The total volume of a reservoir from streambed to maximum operating level
Live (Useful) Storage: The portion of reservoir storage available for operational use, excluding dead storage
Dead Storage: The reservoir volume below minimum operating level, reserved for sediment accumulation
Flow Duration Curve: A graph showing the percentage of time that streamflow equals or exceeds various discharge values
Water Budget (Water Balance): An accounting of all water inflows, outflows, and storage changes in a hydrologic system based on mass conservation
Consumptive Use: Water removed from the immediate source without return, primarily through evapotranspiration
Return Flow: The portion of diverted water not consumed, returning to surface water or groundwater
Duty of Water: The area of land irrigable by a unit discharge flowing continuously for the entire crop base period
Delta: The total depth of water required by a crop during its entire growth period
Consumptive Irrigation Requirement: The crop water need (evapotranspiration) not met by effective rainfall
Gross Irrigation Requirement: The net irrigation requirement divided by application efficiency
Application Efficiency: The fraction of applied irrigation water actually stored in the root zone for plant use
Crop Coefficient (Kc): A factor applied to reference evapotranspiration to estimate actual crop water use at a given growth stage
Reference Evapotranspiration (ET0): The evapotranspiration rate from a standardized reference surface, used as a baseline for crop water calculations
Penman-Monteith Equation: A physically-based method for estimating evapotranspiration combining energy balance and aerodynamic terms
Field Capacity: The amount of soil moisture held after excess water has drained and downward movement has decreased
Permanent Wilting Point: The minimum soil moisture content below which plants cannot extract sufficient water and wilt permanently
Available Water Capacity: The soil moisture range between field capacity and permanent wilting point, available for plant use
Lacey's Regime Theory: A theory for designing stable alluvial irrigation channel dimensions based on discharge and silt factor
Self-Cleansing Velocity: The minimum flow velocity required to prevent sediment deposition in a channel or sewer
Scouring Velocity: The maximum permissible velocity to prevent erosion of channel bed and banks
Sediment Transport: The movement of solid particles by flowing water, encompassing bedload and suspended load
Shields Parameter: A dimensionless number used to determine the threshold condition for initiation of sediment particle movement
Channel Braiding: A river pattern of multiple shifting channels separated by sediment bars, occurring under high sediment load conditions
Channel Meandering: The natural sinuous, curving pattern that develops in alluvial river channels over time
Pier Scour: Localized streambed erosion around a bridge pier foundation due to flow acceleration and vortices
Riprap: Graded rock armor used to protect channel banks and structures from erosion
Channel Degradation: Progressive lowering of a channel bed, often occurring downstream of a dam due to sediment-deficient flow
Wave Celerity: The speed at which a disturbance (flood wave, surge) propagates through a channel, distinct from particle velocity
Water Hammer: A pressure surge caused by sudden changes in flow velocity, such as rapid valve closure
Joukowsky Equation: An equation relating water hammer pressure surge to fluid density, wave celerity, and velocity change, ΔP=ρcΔV
Surge Tank: A structure that absorbs pressure surges and stabilizes flow in a pipeline system
Cavitation: The formation and violent collapse of vapor bubbles due to localized pressure dropping below vapor pressure
NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head): The margin between suction pressure and vapor pressure available to prevent pump cavitation
Specific Speed: A pump parameter combining flow, head, and rotational speed used to classify and select pump impeller type
Pump Affinity Laws: Relationships describing how pump flow, head, and power change with rotational speed
Priming: Filling a centrifugal pump casing and suction line with liquid to remove air before startup
Thrust Block: A structure providing bearing resistance against unbalanced forces at pipe bends and fittings
Minor Losses: Head losses in pipe flow due to fittings, bends, and valves, expressed as hL=K(V²/2g)
Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL): A line representing pressure head plus elevation head along a pipe or channel
Energy Grade Line (EGL): A line representing total energy (pressure, velocity, and elevation head) along a flow path
Hardy Cross Method: An iterative method for analyzing flow distribution in pipe networks
Pipe Network Analysis: The process of determining flow rates and pressures throughout an interconnected pipe system
Non-Revenue Water (NRW): Water produced but lost before reaching customers, generating no revenue
Real (Physical) Losses: Water lost from a distribution system through leaks, breaks, or overflows
Apparent Losses: Water delivered to customers but unaccounted for in revenue, due to meter error or theft
Water Age: The time water spends in a distribution system from treatment to the point of use
Pressure Reducing Valve (PRV): A valve that reduces excessive pressure to a safe operating range in elevation-varied systems
BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand): The amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter over 5 days
COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand): The amount of oxygen required to chemically oxidize organic and inorganic matter in water
Dissolved Oxygen (DO): The concentration of oxygen dissolved in water, essential for aquatic life
Streeter-Phelps Equation: A model describing the dissolved oxygen sag curve downstream of an organic pollution source
Eutrophication: Excessive nutrient enrichment of a water body leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion
Turbidity: The cloudiness of water caused by suspended particles, measured in NTU
Hardness: Water quality measure caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium ions
Alkalinity: The buffering capacity of water against pH changes, primarily from bicarbonate and carbonate
Coagulation: The chemical process of destabilizing colloidal particles in water using coagulants like alum
Flocculation: The process of aggregating destabilized particles into larger, settleable flocs through gentle mixing
Velocity Gradient (G value): A quantifiable measure of mixing intensity in flocculation, related to power input and viscosity
Sedimentation: The settling of suspended particles from water under the influence of gravity
Detention Time: The average time water spends in a treatment tank or basin, calculated as volume divided by flow rate
Rapid Sand Filter: A filtration unit operating at high filtration rates, requiring coagulation pretreatment
Slow Sand Filter: A filtration unit relying on a biological schmutzdecke layer, operating without chemical pretreatment
Backwashing: Reversing flow through a filter at high velocity to remove accumulated solids and restore capacity
Disinfection: The process of inactivating pathogenic microorganisms in water, commonly via chlorination
CT Value: The product of disinfectant concentration and contact time, used to ensure adequate pathogen inactivation
Residual Chlorine: The chlorine remaining in water after disinfection, providing ongoing protection in distribution
Activated Sludge Process: A biological wastewater treatment process using suspended microorganisms to degrade organic matter
Trickling Filter: A fixed-film biological treatment process where wastewater trickles over a media bed
Return Activated Sludge (RAS): Settled biological solids recycled from the clarifier back to the aeration tank
Mixed Liquor Suspended Solids (MLSS): The concentration of suspended solids in the aeration tank of an activated sludge system
Sludge Digestion: Biological stabilization of sludge to reduce volume, pathogens, and odor
Grit Chamber: A unit process removing heavy inorganic solids like sand and gravel through gravity settling
Primary Treatment: Physical wastewater treatment processes removing settleable and floating solids
Secondary Treatment: Biological wastewater treatment processes removing dissolved and colloidal organic matter
Tertiary Treatment: Advanced wastewater treatment achieving higher effluent quality beyond secondary treatment
Membrane Bioreactor (MBR): A wastewater treatment technology combining biological treatment with membrane filtration
Combined Sewer System: A sewer system carrying both sanitary sewage and stormwater in a single pipe
Separate Sewer System: A sewer system using distinct pipes for sanitary sewage and stormwater
Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO): The discharge of untreated combined sewage during heavy rainfall when capacity is exceeded
Infiltration (Sewer): Groundwater entering a sewer system through defective pipes, joints, or manholes
Inflow (Sewer): Stormwater entering a sanitary sewer through direct connections like roof drains
Manhole: An access structure for inspection, cleaning, and maintenance of sewer pipes
Invert Level: The lowest internal point of a pipe's cross-section, governing slope and gravity flow
Detention Basin: A stormwater facility temporarily storing runoff and releasing it at a controlled rate
Retention Basin (Wet Pond): A stormwater facility maintaining a permanent pool providing extended water quality treatment
Green Infrastructure: Stormwater management approaches mimicking natural hydrologic processes, such as bioswales and permeable pavement
First Flush: The phenomenon of disproportionately higher pollutant concentration in the initial portion of stormwater runoff
Level of Service (LOS): A defined performance standard a drainage system is intended to achieve
Time of Concentration: See above; critical parameter for Rational Method design storm duration
Culvert: A structure conveying water under a roadway, embankment, or other obstruction
Inlet Control: Culvert flow condition where capacity is limited by entrance geometry and headwater depth
Outlet Control: Culvert flow condition where capacity is limited by downstream tailwater and barrel friction losses
Fish Ladder (Fishway): A structure allowing migratory fish to pass upstream around a dam or barrier
Environmental Flow: The minimum flow and natural variability maintained in a river to support ecosystem health
Water Rights (Riparian/Prior Appropriation): Legal doctrines governing entitlement to use water from a source
Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM): A coordinated approach managing water, land, and related resources for equitable and sustainable benefit
Non-Stationarity: The recognition that hydrologic statistics may shift over time due to climate or land use change
Sensitivity Analysis: Systematic evaluation of how model outputs change in response to variations in input parameters
Asset Management: Systematic infrastructure condition assessment and risk-based prioritization of investment decisions
Water Footprint: The total volume of water consumed or polluted to produce goods and services, including virtual water
Desalination (Reverse Osmosis): A membrane process removing dissolved salts from seawater or brackish water to produce potable water
Water Reuse: The beneficial use of treated wastewater effluent for irrigation, industrial, or potable applications
SCADA: Supervisory control and data acquisition systems used for monitoring and control of water infrastructure

title: Architecture and Urban Planning Exit Exam Comprehensive Revision Note
content:
Architecture encompasses the art and science of designing and constructing buildings, structures, and environments that meet functional, aesthetic, and cultural needs. It involves the integration of spatial planning, design principles, and construction techniques to create habitable spaces that enhance the quality of life and enrich the built environment
Urban Planning is the discipline of managing and shaping the physical, social, and economic development of cities, towns, and communities. It involves the analysis, design, and implementation of policies, programs, and projects aimed at promoting sustainable urban growth, improving infrastructure, and enhancing the livability, equity, and resilience of urban areas
Architectural Design Principles: Architectural design principles encompass the fundamental concepts and guidelines that govern the creation of buildings and spaces. They include principles such as proportion, scale, balance, rhythm, harmony, and unity, which inform the arrangement, organization, and aesthetics of architectural elements to achieve functional and aesthetic coherence
Urban Design and Planning: Urban design and planning involve the systematic analysis, design, and management of urban spaces, neighborhoods, and regions. It encompasses the development of land use plans, zoning regulations, transportation systems, and public amenities to create sustainable, inclusive, and vibrant urban environments that promote social interaction, economic vitality, and environmental stewardship
Historic Preservation and Conservation: Historic preservation and conservation focus on the identification, protection, and rehabilitation of historic buildings, landmarks, and cultural heritage sites. It involves the documentation, restoration, and adaptive reuse of architectural and archaeological assets to preserve their historical, architectural, and cultural significance for future generations
Sustainable Architecture and Green Building: Sustainable architecture and green building practices aim to minimize the environmental impact of buildings and construction activities while maximizing energy efficiency, resource conservation, and occupant comfort. They involve the use of eco-friendly materials, energy-efficient design strategies, renewable energy systems, and passive design techniques to create buildings that are environmentally responsible and energy-efficient
Landscape Architecture and Urban Greening: Landscape architecture and urban greening focus on the planning, design, and management of outdoor spaces, parks, and green infrastructure within urban areas. They emphasize the integration of natural elements, such as vegetation, water features, and hardscape elements, to enhance biodiversity, mitigate climate change, and improve the quality of urban life
Building Information Modeling (BIM): Building Information Modeling (BIM) is a digital modeling and simulation technology that enables architects, engineers, and construction professionals to collaboratively design, visualize, and analyze building projects in a virtual environment. It facilitates the integration of architectural, structural, and MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) systems, streamlining the design process, reducing errors, and optimizing construction efficiency
Human-Centered Design and Universal Accessibility: Human-centered design and universal accessibility prioritize the needs and experiences of users, including people with disabilities, in the design of buildings, public spaces, and transportation systems. They aim to create environments that are inclusive, accessible, and responsive to the diverse needs and abilities of all individuals, promoting equity, dignity, and social inclusion
Urban Regeneration and Revitalization: Urban regeneration and revitalization initiatives seek to rejuvenate and transform blighted or underutilized urban areas through strategic investments, redevelopment projects, and community engagement efforts. They aim to stimulate economic growth, foster social cohesion, and enhance the quality of life in distressed neighborhoods, revitalizing them as vibrant, sustainable, and resilient urban communities
A bubble diagram: is a diagram that represents information visually in the form of a series of bubbles.  In architecture, the bubble diagram depicts the spatial relationship of areas and rooms within a building and the required circulation routes between these areas
Charrette:An intense and focused design session incorporating collaboration from multiple sources and decision makers
chematic Design (SD):An initial design scheme that seeks to define the general scope and conceptual design of the project including scale and relationships between building components
Finished vs. Unfinished:These terms are used to describe rooms or areas in a home to determine square footage. Unfinished spaces are typically not counted toward square footage and include garages, screened or open patios, porches, and unfinished basement
A site plan: is a specific type of scaled plan which accurately and completely shows the site boundaries, dimensions, and locations of all buildings and structures, uses, and principal site development features, proposed for a specific lot.  A site plan shows means of access to the site, and nearby structures if they are relevant to the design
An elevation is a view of a building seen from one side, a flat representation of one façade. This is the most common view used to describe the external appearance of a building. Each elevation is labeled in relation to the compass direction it faces or by its position relative to the home (e.g. front or rear)
A dormer: is a structure that projects out from a sloped roof. It is often a small room, bedroom, or part of an attic and includes a window
Flashing: is a thin piece of metal that redirects water from a building’s areas that are vulnerable to leaks, including roof valleys, chimneys, skylights, and transitions from exterior wall siding to trim or stone, among others
Muntins are the vertical and horizontal grids used in windows to create divided lites. Muntins extend to a variety of styles and are primarily used to add character and visual interest
A soffit is a material located on the underside of the eave that connects a home’s roof to its outer wall. Soffits come in several different materials and can be vented or unvented. Vented soffits improve a home’s attic ventilation while offering protection against the elements
Urban Infill:The development of the last remaining lots in an existing developed area, the new development within an area already served by existing infrastructure and services, or the reuse of already developed, but vacant properties
Green building is the practice of creating structures and using environmentally responsible and resource-efficient processes throughout a building’s life cycle from siting to design, construction, operation, maintenance, renovation, and deconstruction
Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU):An ADU is a self-contained residential unit that is either attached to or detached from a property’s primary dwelling
Building Envelope: The physical barrier between the interior and exterior environments of a building, encompassing walls, roofs, windows, and doors. It plays a critical role in thermal performance, energy efficiency, and indoor environmental quality
