Addiction Neurobiology: Hijacking of the mesolimbic dopamine reward system; tolerance from neuroadaptation; opponent process producing dysphoria at baseline; incentive salience separating 'wanting' from 'liking'
Reward Prediction Error: Wolfram Schultz's discovery that dopamine neurons signal the difference between expected and actual reward — not reward itself; the neural basis of reinforcement learning
Cognitive Enhancers: Pharmacological and technological methods to improve cognitive performance in healthy individuals; raises neuroethical issues of fairness, coercion, and identity
Neuroethics: The ethics of neuroscience including cognitive enhancement, brain privacy, neuroscience in law, neural interventions, and the definition of personal identity
Free Will Debate: Libet's experiments showing readiness potential preceding conscious intention to move; raises philosophical questions about agency and moral responsibility
Conscious vs. Unconscious Processing: Evidence for extensive non-conscious processing from subliminal priming, blindsight, implicit memory, implicit attitudes, and LeDoux's fast fear pathway
Global Workspace Theory: Baars's theory that consciousness arises when information is 'broadcast' to a widely distributed neural workspace, making it available to multiple cognitive processes simultaneously
Hard Problem of Consciousness: Chalmers's formulation of the difficulty of explaining why physical brain processes give rise to subjective experience
Binding Problem: The neuroscience challenge of explaining how distributed parallel processing of different features is integrated into a unified conscious percept
Inattentional Blindness: Failure to notice unexpected stimuli when attention is engaged elsewhere — demonstrated by the 'invisible gorilla' experiment (Simons and Chabris)
Change Blindness: Failure to notice changes in a scene when the change occurs during a visual disruption
Cocktail Party Effect: The ability to selectively attend to one voice among many while still detecting personally significant information in the unattended channel
Attentional Networks: Posner and Petersen's three networks — Alerting (vigilance, noradrenergic), Orienting (directing attention, parietal-frontal), Executive Control (conflict resolution, ACC and lateral PFC)
Selective Attention: The ability to focus on one stimulus while filtering out others
Divided Attention: Attempting to process two or more streams of information simultaneously — impairs performance on demanding tasks
Embodied Cognition: The proposal that cognition is fundamentally shaped by the body's physical form and sensorimotor interactions — challenging purely computational mind models
Metacognition: Thinking about and regulating one's own cognitive processes; basis for metacognitive therapy (Wells) targeting beliefs about thinking rather than thought content
Cognitive Load Theory: Sweller's framework — working memory has limited capacity; effective instruction minimizes extraneous load, manages intrinsic load, and maximizes germane (schema-building) load
Dual Coding Theory: Paivio's theory that information encoded in both verbal and imagery systems is better remembered than information in only one code
Spaced Repetition: Reviewing material at increasing intervals produces superior long-term retention compared to massed practice — one of the most empirically supported study strategies
Retrieval Practice (Testing Effect): Actively recalling information from memory produces better long-term retention than passive review — more effective than re-reading
Interleaving: Mixing different types of problems or subjects during practice — produces better learning than blocked practice despite feeling more difficult
Desirable Difficulties: Bjork's concept that learning conditions that feel more difficult during study (spacing, interleaving, testing) produce better long-term retention
Cognitive Bias: A systematic pattern of deviation from rational judgment; includes confirmation bias, availability heuristic, representativeness heuristic, anchoring, framing effects, sunk cost fallacy
Confirmation Bias: The tendency to seek, interpret, and remember information that confirms pre-existing beliefs
Availability Heuristic: Judging probability by how easily examples come to mind — leads to overestimating the frequency of dramatic events
Representativeness Heuristic: Judging probability by similarity to a prototype — leads to base rate neglect and the conjunction fallacy
Anchoring: Disproportionate influence of initial information on subsequent judgments
Prospect Theory: Kahneman and Tversky's descriptive theory of decision-making under uncertainty — losses loom larger than equivalent gains (loss aversion ~2:1 ratio); reference points matter
Endowment Effect: The tendency to place greater value on objects one already owns than on equivalent unowned objects — explained by loss aversion
Sunk Cost Fallacy: Continuing to invest in a failing course of action because of past irrecoverable investments
Framing Effect: Decisions influenced by how options are presented (gain vs. loss framing) even when objectively identical
Decision Fatigue: Impaired decision quality and self-regulation after making many successive decisions
Systematic Review: A comprehensive, rigorous synthesis of all available evidence on a specific research question using explicit, reproducible methods
Effect Size: A quantitative measure of the magnitude of a phenomenon or treatment effect; essential for interpreting practical significance beyond statistical significance
Statistical Significance (p-value): The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis were true; p < .05 is the conventional threshold (but does not measure effect size)
Power: The probability of detecting a true effect if it exists; determined by effect size, sample size, and alpha level; low power contributes to replication failure
Race and Intelligence: The debate about whether observed IQ differences between racial groups reflect genetic differences; scientific consensus — primarily explained by environmental, historical, and socioeconomic factors
SexDifferences in Psychology: Most psychological sex differences are small to negligible (Hyde's gender similarities hypothesis); those that exist (mental rotation, physical aggression) are partly culturally modifiable
Intersectionality: Kimberlé Crenshaw's framework recognizing that multiple social identities (race, gender, class) intersect to create unique experiences of privilege and oppression that cannot be understood separately
Psychological Safety: Edmondson's team climate concept where members feel safe to take interpersonal risks; the strongest predictor of team learning and performance in Google's Project Aristotle
Positive Organizational Psychology: Applying positive psychology principles to workplace flourishing — engagement, strengths-based management, psychological safety
Resilience in Organizations: The capacity of organizations to adapt successfully to disruption and adversity while maintaining core functioning
Cognitive Complexity: The degree of differentiation in one's construct system for understanding others — more dimensions, more nuanced social perception (Kelly's personal construct theory)
Self-Complexity: Linville's concept of having many distinct, non-overlapping self-aspects; high self-complexity buffers against mood swings — when one role-based self-aspect is threatened, others remain intact
Psychological Reactance: Brehm's theory — when behavioral freedoms are threatened, people are motivated to restore them, often by doing the opposite of what was demanded
Emotional Intelligence Applied to Therapy: Emotionally intelligent therapists recognize and use their own and clients' emotional signals as clinical data
Virtue Ethics in Psychology: The application of Aristotelian virtue ethics — focusing on character strengths and eudaimonia — to professional practice and ethical decision-making

title: Public Health Science Exit Exam Comprehensive Revision Note
content:
Epidemiology: The study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems. 
 Incidence: The number of new cases of a disease that occur during a specified period of time in a population at risk for developing the disease. 
 Prevalence: The number of affected persons present in the population at a specific time divided by the number of persons in the population at that time. 
 Endemic: The constant presence of a disease or infectious agent within a given geographic area or population group. 
 Epidemic: The occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness, specific health-related behavior, or other health-related events clearly in excess of normal expectancy. 
 Pandemic: An epidemic occurring worldwide, or over a very wide area, crossing international boundaries and usually affecting a large number of people. 
 Zoonosis: An infectious disease that is transmissible under natural conditions from vertebrate animals to humans. 
 Incubation Period: The interval from receipt of infection to the time of onset of clinical illness. 
 Herd Immunity: The resistance of a group of people to an attack by a disease to which a large proportion of the members of the group are immune. 
 Attack Rate: The number of people exposed to a suspect food who became ill divided by the total number of people who were exposed to that food. 
 Case Fatality Rate: The proportion of persons with a particular condition (cases) who die from that condition. 
 Surveillance: The ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data essential to the planning, implementation, and evaluation of public health practice. 
 Sentinel Surveillance: A surveillance system that involves a limited network of carefully selected reporting sites to monitor trends in specific diseases. 
 Contact Tracing: The process of identifying, assessing, and managing people who have been exposed to a disease to prevent onward transmission. 
 Fomite: An inanimate object or substance that is capable of transmitting infectious organisms from one individual to another. 
 Vector: An animate intermediary (like an insect or rodent) in the indirect transmission of an agent that carries the agent from a reservoir to a susceptible host. 
 Natural History of Disease: The course of a disease process from onset to resolution in the absence of intervention. 
 Primary Prevention: Action taken to prevent the development of a disease in a person who is well and does not (yet) have the disease. 
 Secondary Prevention: Identifying people in whom a disease process has already begun but who do not yet have clinical signs or symptoms of the disease (Screening). 
 Tertiary Prevention: Preventing complications in those who already have developed clinical phenomena of an illness. 
 Primordial Prevention: Actions to minimize future hazards to health and hence inhibit the establishment of factors (social, economic, cultural) known to increase the risk of disease. 
Biostatistics: The application of statistics to a wide range of topics in biology and medicine. 
 Mean: The arithmetic average of a distribution, obtained by adding the scores and then dividing by the number of scores. 
 Median: The middle score in a distribution; half the scores are above it and half are below it. 
 Mode: The most frequently occurring score(s) in a distribution. 
 Standard Deviation: A computed measure of how much scores vary around the mean score. 
 P-value: The probability of obtaining the observed results (or more extreme) assuming that the null hypothesis is correct. 
 Confidence Interval: A range of values so defined that there is a specified probability that the value of a parameter lies within it. 
 Null Hypothesis: The hypothesis that there is no significant difference between specified populations, any observed difference being due to sampling or experimental error. 
 Type I Error (Alpha): Rejecting a null hypothesis when it is actually true (False Positive). 
 Type II Error (Beta): Failing to reject a null hypothesis when it is actually false (False Negative). 
 Sensitivity: The ability of a test to correctly identify those with the disease (True Positive Rate). 
 Specificity: The ability of the test to correctly identify those without the disease (True Negative Rate). 
 Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The probability that subjects with a positive screening test truly have the disease. 
 Odds Ratio (OR): A measure of association which compares the odds of disease of those exposed to the odds of disease of those unexposed. 
 Relative Risk (RR): The ratio of the risk of disease in exposed individuals to the risk of disease in unexposed individuals. 
 Confounding: A situation in which the effect or association between an exposure and outcome is distorted by the presence of another variable. 
 Selection Bias: Error due to systematic differences in characteristics between those who take part in a study and those who do not. 
 Recall Bias: Systematic error due to differences in accuracy or completeness of recall to memory of past events or experiences. 
 Cohort Study: A study where two or more groups of people that are free of disease and that differ according to the extent of exposure are compared. 
 Case-Control Study: A study that compares individuals who have a specific disease with individuals who do not have the disease. 
 Cross-Sectional Study: A study that examines the relationship between diseases and other variables of interest as they exist in a defined population at one particular time. 
 Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT): A study in which people are allocated at random to receive one of several clinical interventions. 
 Meta-Analysis: A statistical technique for combining the findings from independent studies. 
The branch of public health that is concerned with all aspects of the natural and built environment that may affect human health. 
 WASH: An acronym that stands for "Water, Sanitation and Hygiene," core pillars of infectious disease control. 
 Chlorination: The process of adding chlorine to drinking water to disinfect it and kill germs. 
 Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD): The amount of dissolved oxygen needed by aerobic biological organisms to break down organic material in a given water sample. 
 Sanitary Landfill: A site where waste is isolated from the environment until it is safe through biological, chemical, and physical processes. 
 Leachate: Any liquid that, in the course of passing through matter, extracts soluble or suspended solids, or any other component of the material through which it has passed. 
 Air Quality Index (AQI): A number used by government agencies to communicate to the public how polluted the air currently is or how polluted it is forecast to become. 
 PM2.5: Atmospheric particulate matter that have a diameter of less than 2.5 micrometers, which can penetrate deep into the lungs. 
 Thermal Inversion: A reversal of the normal behavior of temperature in the troposphere, in which a layer of cool air at the surface is overlaid by a layer of warmer air, trapping pollutants. 
 Greenhouse Effect: The process by which radiation from a planet's atmosphere warms the planet's surface to a temperature above what it would be without its atmosphere. 
 Bio-accumulation: The gradual accumulation of substances, such as pesticides, or other chemicals in an organism. 
 Bio-magnification: The concentration of toxins in an organism as a result of its ingesting other plants or animals in which the toxins are more widely disbursed. 
 Occupational Health: A multidisciplinary field of healthcare concerned with enabling an individual to undertake their occupation, in the way that causes least harm to their health. 
 Ergonomics: The study of people's efficiency in their working environment. 
 Silicosis: Lung fibrosis caused by the inhalation of dust containing silica. 
 Pneumoconiosis: A disease of the lungs due to inhalation of dust, characterized by inflammation, coughing, and fibrosis. 
 Threshold Limit Value (TLV): The level of exposure to a chemical substance or other hazard that a worker can be exposed to daily without adverse effects. 
 Decibel (dB): A unit used to measure the intensity of a sound, used in monitoring occupational noise exposure. 
 Radon: A naturally occurring radioactive gas that can cause lung cancer, often found in basements. 
Health System: The sum total of all the organizations, institutions, and resources whose primary purpose is to improve health. 
 Universal Health Coverage (UHC): Ensuring that all people have access to needed health services of sufficient quality to be effective while also ensuring that the use of these services does not expose the user to financial hardship. 
 Primary Health Care (PHC): Essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods and technology made universally accessible to individuals and families. 
 Alma-Ata Declaration: A 1978 international conference that identified primary health care as the key to attaining the goal of Health for All. 
 Health Policy: Decisions, plans, and actions that are undertaken to achieve specific healthcare goals within a society. 
 Equity: The absence of avoidable or remediable differences among groups of people, whether those groups are defined socially, economically, demographically, or geographically. 
 Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA): A form of economic analysis that compares the relative costs and outcomes of different courses of action. 
 DALY (Disability-Adjusted Life Year): A measure of overall disease burden, expressed as the number of years lost due to ill-health, disability or early death. 
 QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year): A generic measure of disease burden, including both the quality and the quantity of life lived. 
 Fee-for-Service: A payment model where services are unbundled and paid for separately. 
 Capitation: A payment arrangement for health care service providers that pays a set amount for each enrolled person assigned to them, per period of time. 
 Moral Hazard: When the behavior of an insured person changes in a way that raises costs for the insurer (e.g., taking more risks). 
 Adverse Selection: When sicker people are more likely to buy insurance, while healthy people opt out, leading to high premiums. 
 Gross Domestic Product (GDP): The total value of goods produced and services provided in a country during one year. 
 Triage: The assignment of degrees of urgency to wounds or illnesses to decide the order of treatment of a large number of patients. 
 Health Technology Assessment (HTA): A systematic evaluation of properties, effects, and/or impacts of health technology. 
Health Promotion: The process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. 
 Health Education: Any combination of learning experiences designed to help individuals and communities improve their health, by increasing their knowledge or influencing their attitudes. 
 Social Determinants of Health (SDOH): The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age. 
 Health Belief Model (HBM): A psychological model that attempts to explain and predict health behaviors by focusing on the attitudes and beliefs of individuals. 
 Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Change): An integrative theory of therapy that assesses an individual's readiness to act on a new healthier behavior. 
 Self-Efficacy: An individual's belief in their capacity to execute behaviors necessary to produce specific performance attainments. 
 Social Capital: The networks of relationships among people who live and work in a particular society, enabling that society to function effectively. 
 Locus of Control: The degree to which people believe that they, as opposed to external forces, have control over the outcome of events in their lives. 
 Stigma: A mark of disgrace associated with a particular circumstance, quality, or person (e.g., HIV stigma). 
 Health Literacy: The degree to which individuals have the capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information and services needed to make appropriate health decisions. 
 Social Marketing: The use of marketing principles to influence a target audience to voluntarily accept, reject, modify, or abandon a behavior for the benefit of individuals, groups, or society as a whole. 
 Advocacy: A combination of individual and social actions designed to gain political commitment, policy support, social acceptance and systems support for a particular health goal or program. 
Malnutrition: Lack of proper nutrition, caused by not having enough to eat, being unable to use the food that one does eat, or eating the wrong foods. 
 Stunting: Low height-for-age, caused by long-term insufficient nutrient intake and frequent infections. 
 Wasting: Low weight-for-height, indicating recent and severe weight loss. 
 Kwashiorkor: A form of severe protein-energy malnutrition characterized by edema and an enlarged liver with fatty infiltrates. 
 Marasmus: Severe undernourishment causing an infant's or child's weight to be significantly low for their age. 
 Micronutrients: Essential elements required by organisms in varying quantities throughout life to orchestrate a range of physiological functions (Vitamins and Minerals). 
 Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD): A spectrum of health problems including goiter and cretinism resulting from inadequate iodine. 
 Vitamin A Deficiency (VAD): A lack of vitamin A in humans, common in developing countries, leading to blindness and increased mortality from common infections. 
 Bio-fortification: The process of increasing the nutritional value of food crops by increasing the bioavailability of nutrients through plant breeding or genetic engineering. 
 Food Security: When all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. 
 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): A collection of 17 interlinked global goals designed to be a "blueprint to achieve a better and more sustainable future for all" by 2030. 
 Millennium Development Goals (MDGs): Eight international development goals for the year 2015 that had been established following the Millennium Summit of the United Nations in 2000. 
 One Health: An approach to designing and implementing programmes, policies, legislation and research in which multiple sectors communicate and work together to achieve better public health outcomes. 
 Eradication: The permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidence of an infection caused by a specific agent. 
 Elimination: Reduction to zero of the incidence of a specified disease in a defined geographical area. 
 Global Health Security: The activities required, both proactive and reactive, to minimize the danger and impact of acute public health events that endanger people’s health across geographical regions and international boundaries. 
Autonomy: The right of patients to make decisions about their medical care without their healthcare provider trying to influence the decision. 
 Beneficence: The ethical principle that addresses the idea that a nurse's or doctor's actions should promote good. 
 Justice: The principle that all people should be treated fairly and that health resources should be distributed equitably. 
 Informed Consent: A process for getting permission before conducting a healthcare intervention on a person. 
 Paternalism: Action limiting a person's or group's liberty or autonomy which is intended to promote their own good. 
 Harm Principle: The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. 
 Stewardship: The careful and responsible management of something entrusted to one's care (e.g., the government's role in the health system). 
 Confidentiality: The ethical and legal duty of healthcare providers to keep a patient's personal health information private. 
 Quarantine: The restriction of movement of people who may have been exposed to a contagious disease to see if they become sick. 
 Isolation: Separating sick people with a contagious disease from people who are not sick. 
 Forensic Medicine: A branch of medicine that applies medical knowledge to legal issues. 
 Algor Mortis: The second stage of death, is the change in body temperature post mortem, until the ambient temperature is matched. 
 Livor Mortis: A settling of the blood in the lower (dependent) portion of the body post mortem, causing a purplish red discoloration of the skin. 
 Rigor Mortis: One of the recognizable signs of death, caused by chemical changes in the muscles post mortem, which cause the limbs of the corpse to become stiff. 
 Adipocere: A greyish-white fatty substance generated in a corpse when it is kept in moist conditions. 
 Anthropometry: The scientific study of the measurements and proportions of the human body, used in nutrition and forensics. 
Disaster: A serious disruption of the functioning of a community or a society involving widespread human, material, economic or environmental losses and impacts. 
 Hazard: A process, phenomenon or human activity that may cause loss of life, injury or other health impacts. 
 Vulnerability: The conditions determined by physical, social, economic and environmental factors or processes which increase the susceptibility of an individual or community to the impacts of hazards. 
 Risk: The probability of harmful consequences, or expected losses resulting from interactions between natural or human-induced hazards and vulnerable conditions. 
 Mitigation: The lessening or minimizing of the adverse impacts of a hazardous event. 
 Preparedness: The knowledge and capacities developed by governments, response and recovery organizations, communities and individuals to effectively anticipate, respond to and help family and community recover from the impacts of likely, imminent or current disasters. 
 Resilience: The ability of a system, community or society exposed to hazards to resist, absorb, accommodate, adapt to, transform and recover from the effects of a hazard in a timely and efficient manner. 
 Surge Capacity: The ability of a health system to expand rapidly beyond normal services to meet the increased demand for qualified personnel, medical care, and public health in the event of a large-scale emergency. 
 Rapid Needs Assessment: A survey conducted immediately after a disaster to identify the most urgent needs of the affected population. 
 Drought: A deficiency of precipitation over an extended period, resulting in a water shortage. 
Incubator: An apparatus in which environmental conditions, such as temperature and humidity, are controlled, often used for growing bacterial cultures or maintaining premature babies. 
 Reservoir: Any person, animal, plant, soil or substance in which an infectious agent normally lives and multiplies. 
 Carrier: A person or animal that transmits a disease-causing organism to others, especially without suffering from it themselves. 
 Vertical Program: A health program that focuses on a single disease (e.g., Polio eradication) rather than the whole health system. 
 Horizontal Program: A health program that aims to strengthen the general health system rather than focusing on a specific disease. 
 Integrated Disease Surveillance (IDSR): A strategy for strengthening national public health surveillance and response systems. 
 Mortality: The state of being subject to death. 
 Morbidity: The condition of being diseased. 
 Demography: The study of statistics such as births, deaths, income, or the incidence of disease, which illustrate the changing structure of human populations. 
 Dependency Ratio: An age-population ratio of those typically not in the labor force and those typically in the labor force. 
 Life Expectancy: A statistical measure of the average time an organism is expected to live, based on the year of its birth, its current age and other demographic factors. 
 Replacement Level Fertility: The total fertility rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration.

title: Sociology Exit Exam Comprehensive Revision Note
content:
Society: The system of human organizations and institutions, creating a complex whole in which individuals are embedded and shaped
Sociology: The scientific study of society, social behavior, social groups, institutions, and how they interact and change over time
Sociological Imagination: C. Wright Mills' concept connecting personal biography to broader social and historical forces
Social Structure: The organized patterns of relationships and social institutions that shape society
Social Institution: A complex of established norms, roles, and practices addressing fundamental social needs (family, education, religion, economy, state)
Social Norms: Shared rules and expectations about appropriate behavior in social situations
Folkways: Everyday conventions with mild sanctions for violations (etiquette, dress codes)
Mores: Norms essential to morality and group welfare with stronger sanctions (taboos against murder)
Taboos: Strongly prohibited behaviors within a culture, violations of which produce intense social condemnation
Laws: Formally codified norms enforced by the state through official sanctions
Social Sanctions: Rewards or punishments used to enforce social norms
Values: Deeply held beliefs about what is good, right, and desirable in society
Culture: The shared beliefs, values, norms, symbols, language, and practices of a group or society
Material Culture: Physical objects, artifacts, and technology created and used by a society
Non-Material Culture: Intangible aspects of culture including beliefs, values, norms, and language
Cultural Relativism: Understanding cultural practices within their own cultural context rather than judging them by another culture's standards
Ethnocentrism: Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own culture
Cultural Diffusion: The spread of cultural elements from one society to another
Cultural Lag: The gap between technological change and social/cultural adaptation
Subculture: A group within a larger culture with distinctive norms, values, and practices
Counterculture: A subculture that actively opposes dominant cultural values and norms
Cultural Hegemony: Gramsci's concept describing how dominant class worldviews are reproduced through cultural institutions
Ideology: A system of ideas and ideals that form the basis of economic or political thinking
False Consciousness: Marx's concept where workers fail to recognize their objective class interests and accept ruling class ideology
Hegemony: Gramsci's concept of how dominant groups maintain power through cultural leadership and consent rather than force
Organic Intellectuals: Gramsci's concept of intellectuals who emerge from and articulate the worldview of a social class
Traditional Intellectuals: Intellectuals who appear neutral but actually serve dominant class interests
Counter-Hegemony: Cultural and political challenges to dominant hegemonic frameworks
Socialization: The lifelong process through which individuals learn culture, norms, values, roles, and identities
Primary Socialization: Early childhood socialization through the family acquiring language, values, and basic self-concept
Secondary Socialization: Socialization throughout life in institutions beyond the family (school, peers, media, workplace)
Resocialization: The process of dismantling prior socialization and replacing it with new norms (total institutions, religious conversion)
Agents of Socialization: Key institutions that transmit culture (family, peer groups, schools, media, religion, workplace)
Social Role: A set of expected behaviors, rights, and obligations associated with a social position
Role Conflict: Tension arising when an individual occupies multiple positions with incompatible expectations
Role Strain: Tension within a single role when the role itself contains contradictory demands
Role Exit: Ebaugh's concept describing the process of disengaging from a central identity role
Ascribed Status: Status assigned at birth or involuntarily (race, sex, family background)
Achieved Status: Status acquired through personal effort, ability, or choice (occupation, educational level)
Master Status: A status that overrides all others in shaping social identity (disability, race, criminal record)
Status Inconsistency: Lenski's concept where an individual ranks differently across multiple stratification dimensions
Social Stratification: The hierarchical arrangement of people into layers with unequal access to resources, power, and prestige
Social Class: Groupings based primarily on economic position including income, wealth, and occupational prestige
Caste System: A rigid, hereditary system of social stratification based on birth
Slavery: An extreme form of stratification in which persons are legally owned as property
Feudal Estates: Medieval European hierarchy of nobility, clergy, and commons tied to land
Bourgeoisie: Marx's term for the capitalist class that owns the means of production
Proletariat: Marx's term for the working class that sells its labor power for wages
Petty Bourgeoisie: Small business owners and self-employed individuals occupying an intermediate class position
Class Consciousness: Marx's concept of workers' awareness of their shared class interests and exploitation
Class in Itself: Marx's concept of an objective economic position shared by people without collective identity
Class for Itself: Marx's concept of a class that has developed collective identity and political organization
Surplus Value: Marx's concept of the difference between the value workers create and the wages they receive
Alienation: Marx's concept of workers' estrangement from products, productive process, species-being, and other workers
Means of Production: The physical and social factors necessary for producing goods (land, tools, factories, capital)
Relations of Production: Social relationships people enter into when producing goods under capitalism
Mode of Production: The combination of forces and relations of production in a given historical era
Base and Superstructure: Marx's model where economic base shapes cultural and political superstructure
Historical Materialism: Marx's theory that material/economic conditions determine social development
Capital: Wealth used to generate more wealth through investment and the employment of labor
Capitalism: An economic system based on private ownership of means of production and production for profit
Neoliberalism: A political-economic ideology promoting free markets, deregulation, privatization, and individual responsibility as both policy and cultural project
Globalization: The process by which the world becomes increasingly interconnected through trade, communication, and cultural exchange
World-Systems Theory: Wallerstein's theory of global capitalist economy organized into core, semi-periphery, and periphery nations
Dependency Theory: Theory arguing that Global South poverty results from exploitation by core nations rather than internal deficiencies
McDonaldization: Ritzer's concept describing the spread of fast-food principles (efficiency, calculability, predictability, control) to all social domains
Glocalization: Robertson's concept that global processes are always adapted and localized rather than homogenizing cultures
Cultural Imperialism: The dominance of powerful nations' cultures displacing local cultures through global media and consumer culture
Postcolonialism: Theoretical framework analyzing the lasting effects of colonialism on societies, cultures, and knowledge systems
Orientalism: Said's concept of how Western knowledge constructs the East as exotic, irrational, and inferior to justify colonialism
Hybridity: Bhabha's concept of the mixed, unstable cultural identities produced through colonial encounters
Southern Theory: Connell's argument that sociology must include non-Western intellectual traditions rather than universalizing European theory
Social Mobility: Movement between social class positions
Absolute Social Mobility: How many people actually move to different class positions from their parents
Relative Social Mobility: Whether people from different class backgrounds have equal chances of reaching top positions
Intergenerational Mobility: Social mobility across generations (comparing parents and children)
Intragenerational Mobility: Social mobility within a single generation or lifetime
Meritocracy: The belief that social positions are allocated based on individual talent and effort
Credentialism: Collins' concept of the increasing reliance on educational credentials as qualifications regardless of skill requirements
Credential Inflation: As more people obtain qualifications their positional value declines requiring ever-higher credentials
Cultural Capital: Bourdieu's concept of knowledge, skills, tastes, and competencies that confer social advantages
Embodied Cultural Capital: Cultural capital in the form of durable dispositions and habits
Objectified Cultural Capital: Cultural capital in the form of cultural goods (books, art, instruments)
Institutionalized Cultural Capital: Cultural capital in the form of academic credentials
Social Capital: Networks of mutual recognition and social connections that can be mobilized as resources
Bonding Social Capital: Strong ties within homogeneous groups creating solidarity but potential exclusion
Bridging Social Capital: Weaker ties across diverse groups enabling access to wider resources and opportunities
Economic Capital: Financial resources including income and accumulated wealth
Symbolic Capital: Recognized and legitimated forms of capital that confer prestige and authority
Habitus: Bourdieu's concept of a system of durable dispositions shaped by social position that guide perception and action
Field: Bourdieu's concept of a structured social space with its own rules, positions, and forms of valued capital
Practice: Bourdieu's concept of everyday social action produced through the interaction of habitus and field
Distinction: Bourdieu's analysis of how cultural tastes function as markers of social class difference
Symbolic Violence: Bourdieu's concept of the gentle, invisible form of power exercised through misrecognition
Misrecognition: Bourdieu's concept of the process through which class privilege appears as natural talent
Cleft Habitus: Bourdieu's concept of the split experience of upwardly mobile individuals between two class worlds
Illusio: Bourdieu's term for the shared belief in what is worth competing for within a field
Capital Conversion: The process through which one form of capital is transformed into another
Reproduction in Education: Bourdieu and Passeron's analysis of how schools reproduce class inequality through cultural capital
Social Reproduction: The processes through which existing social structures and inequalities are maintained across generations
Social Reproduction Theory: Feminist Marxist theory analyzing how unpaid care work reproduces labor power for capitalism
Patriarchy: A system of social structures and practices in which men dominate, oppress, and exploit women
Sex: Biological characteristics that distinguish males and females
Gender: The socially and culturally constructed meanings, identities, and roles associated with biological sex
Gender Performativity: Butler's concept that gender is not an expression of inner essence but constituted through repeated stylized acts
Heterosexual Matrix: Butler's term for the cultural grid requiring sex, gender, and desire to align in coherent ways
Compulsory Heterosexuality: Rich's concept that heterosexuality is a political institution imposed as the natural form of sexuality
Heteronormativity: The assumption that heterosexuality is the natural normal and default form of sexuality embedded in social institutions
Queer Theory: A theoretical framework challenging the normalization of social categories especially around sexuality and gender
Hegemonic Masculinity: Connell's concept of the culturally dominant form of masculinity that legitimates male dominance
Patriarchal Dividend: Connell's term for the advantages men receive from the overall subordination of women
Second Shift: Hochschild's concept of the unpaid domestic work women primarily perform after paid employment
Emotional Labor: Hochschild's concept of the management of feeling to fulfill the emotional requirements of a job
Aesthetic Labor: Warhurst and Nickson's concept of employers requiring workers to embody particular aesthetic styles as part of the job
Feminization of Poverty: The disproportionate concentration of poverty among women due to structural factors
Gender Pay Gap: The systematic difference in average earnings between men and women
Occupational Segregation: The concentration of men and women in different occupations or hierarchical levels
Horizontal Segregation: The concentration of men and women in different types of occupations
Vertical Segregation: The concentration of men at the top and women at the bottom of organizational hierarchies
Glass Ceiling: The invisible barrier preventing women from advancing to senior positions
Motherhood Penalty: The disadvantage in earnings and career advancement experienced by mothers
Fatherhood Bonus: The advantage in earnings and career advancement experienced by fathers
Care Work: Paid and unpaid work involved in caring for others (childcare, eldercare, emotional support)
Global Care Chain: Hochschild's concept of transnational circuits of care labor connecting wealthy and poor countries
Feminist Standpoint Theory: Smith and Harding's argument that knowledge is always produced from a particular social standpoint
Intersectionality: Crenshaw's concept that race, class, and gender do not operate independently but mutually constitute each other
Matrix of Domination: Collins' concept of interlocking systems of oppression (race, class, gender) operating at multiple levels
Testimonial Injustice: Fricker's concept of giving someone less credibility due to prejudice about their social identity
Hermeneutical Injustice: Fricker's concept of being disadvantaged in understanding one's own experience due to gaps in interpretive resources
Epistemic Injustice: Fricker's broader concept of wrongs done to people specifically in their capacity as knowers
Double Consciousness: Du Bois's concept of the divided sense of self experienced by Black Americans seeing themselves through white society's eyes
The Veil: Du Bois's metaphor for the barrier of race separating Black and white America
Race: A socially constructed category based on perceived physical differences with real social consequences
Racialization: The process by which groups and practices come to be defined and classified in racial terms
Racial Formation Theory: Omi and Winant's theory that race is continuously created through historical social processes (racial projects)
Institutional Racism: Policies, practices, and procedures producing racially unequal outcomes regardless of individual intentions
Color-blind Racism: Bonilla-Silva's concept of racism operating without explicit bigotry through ostensibly race-neutral principles
Colorism: Discrimination based on skin tone within a racial group
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between language or behavioral styles to conform to dominant group norms
White Privilege: The unearned advantages conferred to white people by virtue of their race
Contact Hypothesis: Allport's theory that intergroup contact reduces prejudice under specific conditions (equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support)
Prejudice: A preconceived opinion usually unfavorable about a group based on stereotypes
Discrimination: The unequal behavioral treatment of people based on group membership
Stereotype Threat: Steele's concept of the performance impairment caused by awareness of negative stereotypes about one's group
Poverty: The condition of having insufficient resources for an adequate standard of living
Absolute Poverty: Poverty defined in terms of minimum physical survival requirements
Relative Poverty: Townsend's concept of poverty as inability to participate in the normal life of one's society
Social Exclusion: The multidimensional process by which individuals are shut out from full social participation
Culture of Poverty: Lewis's controversial theory that the poor develop a distinct subculture perpetuating poverty across generations
Vicious Circle of Poverty: The self-reinforcing process by which poverty generates conditions that reproduce poverty
Poverty Trap: A situation where taking paid employment leaves a person no better off than remaining on benefits
Wealth Inequality: The unequal distribution of assets, property, and savings across social groups
Material Deprivation: The lack of physical resources needed for basic human needs and social participation
Working Poor: Individuals who are employed but still live below the poverty line
Precariat: Standing's concept of a new class formation characterized by chronic insecurity and lack of labor rights
Uncertain Employment: Work arrangements lacking security, benefits, and stable income (gig work, zero-hours contracts)
Deindustrialization: The decline of manufacturing industries and the economic and social consequences for affected communities
Surplus Population: Marx's concept of the unemployed and underemployed pool maintaining capitalist labor discipline
Demography: The statistical study of population including size, composition, and spatial distribution
Fertility Rate: The average number of children born per woman in a population
Mortality Rate: The frequency of death in a defined population
Demographic Transition: The historical shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates
Demographic Dividend: The economic growth potential from having a large working-age population relative to dependents
Urbanization: The movement of population from rural areas to cities
Suburbanization: The movement of population from city centers to surrounding suburban areas
Gentrification: The process by which wealthier residents move into lower-income urban neighborhoods raising property values and displacing existing residents
Right to the City: Lefebvre and Harvey's concept of the collective right to participate in and transform urban life
Social Production of Space: Lefebvre's theory that space is socially produced through physical, mental, and social dimensions
Concentric Zone Model: Burgess's Chicago School model of urban structure with zones of distinctive land use
Social Disorganization Theory: The theory that high crime results from the breakdown of informal social control in urban transitional zones
Collective Efficacy: Sampson's concept of neighborhood social cohesion and willingness to intervene for social control
Migration: The movement of people from one place to another
Push Factors: Conditions driving people from their place of origin (poverty, conflict, environmental disaster)
Pull Factors: Conditions attracting people to a destination (economic opportunity, safety, family connections)
Transnationalism: The phenomenon of migrants maintaining simultaneous ties in both origin and destination countries
Assimilation: The process by which immigrants progressively adopt the culture of their host society
Segmented Assimilation: Portes and Zhou's theory that different immigrant groups assimilate into different segments of society
Multiculturalism: A policy and ideology recognizing and valuing diverse cultural traditions within one polity
Diaspora: A dispersed population sharing common origins living outside their homeland
Feminization of Migration: The increased proportion and significance of women in international migration
Sociology of Education: The study of how educational institutions reproduce and sometimes challenge social inequalities
Hidden Curriculum: Jackson's concept of unofficial lessons transmitted through school organization beyond formal academic content
Correspondence Principle: Bowles and Gintis's argument that the social relations of schooling correspond to the social relations of capitalist production
Tracking/Streaming: The practice of placing students into different educational pathways based on perceived ability
Meritocracy in Education: The belief that educational success reflects individual talent and effort rather than social background
Matthew Effect: Merton's concept (extended by Stanovich) that early advantages compound over time producing growing inequality
Pygmalion Effect: Rosenthal and Jacobson's finding that teacher expectations function as self-fulfilling prophecies
Biographical Availability: McAdam's concept of having few competing obligations that would raise the costs of activism
Secularization Thesis: The theory that modernization inevitably leads to declining religious belief and practice
Desecularization: Berger's revised concept that modernization does not necessarily produce secularization
Civil Religion: Bellah's concept of quasi-religious beliefs and rituals surrounding the nation itself
Vicarious Religion: Davie's concept of belief without belonging in contemporary European religiosity
Collective Effervescence: Durkheim's concept of the heightened emotional state generated when people gather in collective rituals
Sacred and Profane: Durkheim's fundamental distinction between things set apart and forbidden versus ordinary everyday objects
Totemism: Durkheim's concept of an object representing the collective identity of a social group
Church-Sect Typology: Troeltsch and Wallis's framework distinguishing institutionalized churches from breakaway sects
New Religious Movements: Emergent religious organizations arising in periods of social change
Religious Market Theory: Stark and Bainbridge's rational choice approach to religious vitality through denominational competition
Anomic: Durkheim's concept of a weakening of collective norms and shared values
Mechanical Solidarity: Durkheim's concept of social cohesion based on similarity in traditional societies
Organic Solidarity: Durkheim's concept of social cohesion based on functional interdependence in modern societies
Division of Labor: The specialization of tasks in society or production
Collective Consciousness: Durkheim's concept of shared beliefs, ideas, and moral attitudes unifying a society
Social Facts: Durkheim's concept of ways of acting, thinking, and feeling external to individuals and exercising constraint over them
Anomie: Durkheim's concept of insufficient social regulation producing normlessness
Egoistic Suicide: Durkheim's type caused by insufficient integration with society
Altruistic Suicide: Durkheim's type caused by excessive integration leading to self-sacrifice
Anomic Suicide: Durkheim's type caused by insufficient social regulation during rapid change
Fatalistic Suicide: Durkheim's type caused by excessive regulation and oppression
Rationalization: Weber's concept of the replacement of tradition and values with rational calculation and efficiency
Iron Cage: Weber's metaphor for the dehumanizing trap of excessive bureaucratic rationalization
Disenchantment: Weber's concept of the loss of magic and meaning as scientific rationality replaces tradition
Bureaucracy: Weber's ideal type of rationalized organizational structure based on rules, hierarchy, and expertise
Legal-Rational Authority: Weber's type of legitimate authority based on rationally enacted rules and expertise
Traditional Authority: Weber's type of legitimate authority based on immemorial tradition
Charismatic Authority: Weber's type of legitimate authority based on exceptional personal qualities
Social Action: Weber's concept of action oriented toward the meanings and actions of others
Verstehen: Weber's method of empathetic understanding of the subjective meanings of social action
The Protestant Ethic: Weber's thesis linking Calvinist values to the spirit of capitalism
De-Sacralization: The process by which the sacred loses its social power and special status
Status Group: Weber's concept of groups sharing similar social honor, prestige, and lifestyle
Life Chances: Weber's concept of the opportunities individuals have for a better quality of life
Three Dimensions of Stratification: Weber's analysis of class (economic), status (prestige), and party (power) as distinct axes
Simmel's Formal Sociology: Simmel's approach identifying recurring patterns of interaction across different social contents
The Stranger: Simmel's concept of a person who is near yet far, inside yet outside, enabling objectivity
Dyad: Simmel's concept of a two-person group with unique social properties
Triad: Simmel's concept of a three-person group that changes social dynamics significantly
Metropolis: Simmel's analysis of how urban life shapes a distinctive blasé, calculating social psychology
Conspicuous Consumption: Veblen's concept of consumption primarily for social signaling of status
Veblen Good: A good whose demand increases as its price rises because the high price is the status signal
Gemeinschaft: Tönnies's concept of community based on organic personal bonds, shared customs, and kinship
Gesellschaft: Tönnies's concept of association based on rational, contractual, impersonal, interest-based bonds
Parsons' AGIL Scheme: Four functional prerequisites (Adaptation, Goal Attainment, Integration, Latency) for any social system
Structural Functionalism: The theoretical perspective analyzing society as a system of interrelated parts maintaining stability
Manifest Functions: Merton's concept of intended and recognized consequences of social patterns
Latent Functions: Merton's concept of unintended and unrecognized consequences of social patterns
Dysfunctions: Merton's concept of social patterns having negative consequences undermining stability
Functionalist Critique: The charge that functionalism has conservative bias justifying existing social arrangements as necessary
Conflict Theory: The theoretical perspective emphasizing social conflict, power inequality, and social change
Strain Theory: Merton's theory that crime results from the gap between culturally prescribed goals and available legitimate means
Conformity: Merton's adaptation accepting both cultural goals and legitimate means
Innovation: Merton's adaptation accepting goals but using illegitimate means (crime)
Ritualism: Merton's adaptation abandoning success goals but continuing following legitimate rules
Retreatism: Merton's adaptation abandoning both goals and means (chronic substance abuse, vagrancy)
Rebellion: Merton's adaptation rejecting existing goals and means and substituting new ones
Self-Fulfilling Prophecy: Merton's concept where a false definition of a situation produces behavior making it come true
Thomas Theorem: If people define situations as real they are real in their consequences
Symbolic Interactionism: The theoretical perspective emphasizing the meanings people attach to objects and actions in social interaction
Looking-Glass Self: Cooley's concept of self-concept emerging from imagining how we appear to others and their reactions
Generalized Other: Mead's concept of the internalized attitudes and expectations of the whole community
Play Stage: Mead's developmental stage where children take the role of specific others
Game Stage: Mead's developmental stage where children must simultaneously coordinate multiple roles
I and Me: Mead's distinction between the spontaneous acting self (I) and the socialized self reflecting society's expectations (Me)
Role-Taking: Mead's concept of imagining another's perspective as prerequisite for selfhood
Definition of the Situation: The subjective interpretation of a social situation that shapes behavior
Impression Management: Goffman's concept of the effort to control how others perceive us through our performances
Dramaturgical Perspective: Goffman's theatrical metaphor treating social life as performance
Front Stage: Goffman's concept of the region where performances occur for audiences
Back Stage: Goffman's concept of where actors prepare, relax, and step out of character
Frame Analysis: Goffman's concept of the interpretive schemata used to make sense of social situations
Stigma: Goffman's concept of a deeply discrediting attribute reducing the bearer to a tainted, discounted person
Totalization: Goffman's concept of how total institutions systematically strip away normal identity
Total Institution: Goffman's concept of an institution encompassing all aspects of residents' lives (prison, mental hospital, military)
Moral Career: Goffman's concept of the sequence of changes in self-concept as one moves through social institutions
Face Work: Goffman's concept of practices used to present a positive self-image and protect social reputation
Stigma Management: Goffman's analysis of how stigmatized individuals conceal or disclose their discrediting attributes
Ethnomethodology: Garfinkel's approach studying the practical methods people use to accomplish everyday social interaction
Breaching Experiments: Garfinkel's method of deliberately violating everyday norms to reveal their invisible structure
Indexicality: Garfinkel's concept that the meaning of expressions is inseparably tied to context of use
Conversation Analysis: Sacks, Schegloff, and Jefferson's analysis of the sequential organization of talk-in-interaction
Adjacency Pairs: CA concept of paired conversational actions (question/answer, greeting/greeting)
Turn-Taking: CA concept of the systematic organization of conversational turns
Preference Organization: CA concept that some responses are preferred (agreement) while others are dispreferred (disagreement)
Double Hermeneutic: Giddens' concept that sociological findings feed back into the social world changing what they describe
Structuration Theory: Giddens' theory that structure and agency are mutually constituting through social practices
Ontological Security: Giddens' concept of a basic sense of trust in the continuity of self-identity and social world
Reflexive Modernization: Beck and Giddens' concept that modernity now reflects upon and reforms itself
Liquid Modernity: Bauman's concept that solid social structures have dissolved into fluid, individual-choice-based conditions
Individualization: Beck and Giddens' concept of the biographical liberation from traditional social structures
Risk Society: Beck's concept that modernity generates manufactured global risks threatening the systems producing them
Pure Relationship: Giddens' concept of a relationship continued only for what each partner derives from it
Narrative Identity: Ricoeur's and Giddens' concept that selfhood is constituted through ongoing biographical narrative construction
Project of the Self: Giddens' concept of identity as an ongoing reflexive project requiring continuous construction
Postmodernism: The theoretical stance rejecting grand narratives and universal truth claims
Grand Narratives: Lyotard's term for overarching stories about history's progressive direction (Enlightenment, Marxism)
Simulacra: Baudrillard's concept of copies without originals that characterize consumer society
Hyperreality: Baudrillard's concept of a media-saturated reality more real than reality itself
Post-Industrial Society: Bell's concept of a society where the economy shifts from manufacturing to services and information
Knowledge Economy: An economy where knowledge, information, and intellectual capital are primary drivers of productivity
Surveillance Capitalism: Zuboff's concept of tech companies extracting and commodifying behavioral data for commercial modification
Digital Labor: Terranova's concept of the uncompensated work performed by users creating value for digital platforms
Platform Capitalism: Srnicek's concept of business models organized around digital platforms extracting value through data
Algorithm: A computational procedure that can reproduce, amplify, or challenge social inequalities at scale
Filter Bubble: Pariser's concept of personalized information environments produced by algorithmic curation
Digital Divide: Structural barriers producing unequal access to and benefit from digital technologies
Social Media: Digital platforms enabling user-generated content, networking, and social interaction
Connective Action: Bennett and Segerberg's concept of digitally enabled personal-action political participation
Social Network Analysis: The mapping and analysis of relationships between actors in a social system
Network Society: Castells' concept of a society whose social structure is built around digital information networks
Space of Flows: Castells' concept of the global network of capital, information, and power flows
Slacktivism: Low-commitment digital participation that does not translate into sustained political action
Virtual Ethnography: The application of ethnographic methods to online communities and digital spaces
Sociology of Science: The study of how social factors shape the production of scientific knowledge
Paradigm: Kuhn's concept of a shared scientific framework of assumptions, methods, and exemplary problems
Scientific Revolution: Kuhn's concept of a revolutionary change in dominant scientific paradigm
Actor-Network Theory: Latour and Callon's framework including non-human actors in social analysis
Social Construction of Technology: Bijker and Pinch's argument that technologies are shaped by social interests and negotiations
Laboratory Life: Latour and Woolgar's ethnographic analysis revealing the social construction of scientific facts
Scientific Controversies: Collins' analysis of how scientific facts are socially negotiated in contested research areas
Sociology of Professions: Analysis of how occupations achieve monopolistic control over knowledge domains
Professional Dominance: Freidson's concept of medicine's privileged position through social closure
Epistemic Communities: Haas's concept of networks of experts sharing knowledge and policy-relevant frameworks
Sociology of the Body: The subfield examining how the body is socially shaped, regulated, and given meaning
Docile Bodies: Foucault's concept of bodies produced by modern disciplinary institutions as simultaneously capable and obedient
Biopower: Foucault's concept of modern power's investment in managing and optimizing life itself
Biopolitics: Foucault's concept of power governing populations through statistics and public health
Governmentality: Foucault's concept of rationalities and techniques for governing populations including subjects themselves
Panopticon: Bentham's prison design used by Foucault as a model of modern surveillance producing self-discipline
Normalization: Foucault's concept of the process of comparing individuals to norms and classifying deviation
Discourse: Foucault's concept of systems of knowledge and power defining what can be said and known in a domain
Archeology: Foucault's historical method analyzing the conditions making specific knowledge systems possible
Genealogy: Foucault's critical historical method tracing contingent, power-laden origins of taken-for-granted truths
Body Project: Shilling's concept of the body as a project of identity construction in late modernity
Embodiment: The ways in which the body is shaped by and expressive of social structures and cultural meanings
Sexuality: The socially organized system of erotic desires, identities, and practices
Heterosexuality: Sexual orientation toward persons of a different sex, socially constructed as the normative default
Homosexuality: Sexual orientation toward persons of the same sex
Bisexuality: Sexual attraction to both men and women
Transgender: A person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth
Neurodiversity: The concept that neurological differences (autism, ADHD) are natural human variations deserving accommodation
Disability: Social model perspective that disability is produced by society's failure to accommodate human diversity
Social Model of Disability: The framework distinguishing impairment (bodily difference) from disability (social barriers)
Medical Model of Disability: The framework locating disability in individual bodily or mental conditions requiring cure
Ableism: Discrimination and social prejudice against people with disabilities
Agism: Discrimination and stereotyping based on age
Deviance: Behavior that violates social norms and expectations
Primary Deviance: Lemert's concept of initial rule-breaking before labeling
Secondary Deviance: Lemert's concept of rule-breaking that develops as a response to being labeled deviant
Labeling Theory: The theory that deviance is not inherent in acts but created by social reactions and labels
Moral Entrepreneurs: Becker's concept of individuals or groups who campaign to have behaviors defined as deviant
Differential Association Theory: Sutherland's theory that criminal behavior is learned through interaction with deviant others
Social Bond Theory: Hirschi's theory that delinquency occurs when bonds to conventional society weaken
Neutralization Techniques: Sykes and Matza's five rationalizations allowing offenders to maintain conventional self-concepts
Folk Devils: Cohen's concept of groups becoming symbolically associated with all that is wrong with society
Moral Panic: Cohen's concept of exaggerated, disproportionate social concern about a perceived threat
Deviance Amplification: The process by which media coverage increases deviant behavior through labeling and attention
White-Collar Crime: Sutherland's concept of crime committed by persons of high social status in their occupational roles
Penal Populism: Pratt's concept of politically driven punitive policies responding to public fear rather than evidence
Mass Incarceration: The extremely high rate of imprisonment in the US affecting predominantly Black and poor communities
Restorative Justice: Braithwaite's approach focusing on repairing harm and reintegrating offenders rather than punishing
Reintegrative Shaming: Braithwaite's concept of expressing disapproval of acts while affirming the person
Medicalization: The process by which behaviors previously treated as moral failures come to be defined as medical conditions
De-medicalization: The process by which conditions previously classified as medical are reclassified
Social Epidemiology: The study of the social distribution of health and illness
Social Determinants of Health: The social conditions (income, education, housing, work) primarily shaping health outcomes
Social Gradient of Health: The finding that health outcomes improve at every step up the social hierarchy
Allostatic Load: The cumulative biological cost of chronic stress from social disadvantage
Sick Role: Parsons' concept of illness as a social role with rights (exemption from duties) and obligations (seek help, want recovery)
Biographical Disruption: Bury's concept that chronic illness disrupts the taken-for-granted foundations of everyday life
Narrative Reconstruction: The process of developing a coherent account of illness within one's life story
Emotional Geography: The understanding that social spaces are coded with emotional meanings unequally accessible by social position
Global Care Chain: Hochschild's concept of transnational chains of care work connecting wealthy and poor countries
Environmental Racism: Bullard's concept of the disproportionate placement of environmental hazards in communities of color
Environmental Justice: The movement and framework arguing environmental hazards and benefits are unequally distributed
Treadmill of Production: Schnaiberg's concept that capitalism requires continuous growth demanding increasing resource extraction
Metabolic Rift: Foster's Marxist concept of capitalism's fundamental disruption of ecological cycles
Risk Society: Beck's concept of a modernity organized around the management of manufactured global risks
Social Movements: Organized, sustained collective efforts to bring about social change
Resource Mobilization Theory: McCarthy and Zald's theory that movement success depends on organizational resources
Political Opportunity Structure: Tarrow's concept of the political context shaping movement emergence and success
Framing Theory: Snow and Benford's analysis of how movements strategically define problems, diagnose causes, and motivate action
Collective Identity: Melucci's concept of the shared definition of who we are as a movement sustaining participation
New Social Movement Theory: European theory emphasizing identity, cultural politics, and post-material values
Free Rider Problem: Olson's concept that rational individuals will benefit from collective goods without contributing
Transnational Advocacy Networks: Keck and Sikkink's concept of cross-border activist networks influencing policy
Welfare State: The system of state provision protecting citizens against major life risks
Esping-Andersen's Three Worlds: Liberal, conservative-corporatist, and social-democratic welfare state types
Decommodification: Esping-Andersen's concept of the degree to which people can maintain livelihoods without relying on the market
Welfare Chauvinism: The political position that social benefits should be restricted to ethnic insiders
Austerity: Government spending cuts that restructure the social contract shifting risks onto individuals especially women
Public Sphere: Habermas's concept of a space of rational-critical debate where private citizens reason about public affairs
Subaltern Counterpublics: Fraser's concept of alternative discursive arenas where subordinated groups develop counter-discourses
Deliberative Democracy: Habermas's normative ideal of democracy based on genuine public rational deliberation
Civil Society: The arena of voluntary associations between the state and the family providing space for civic engagement
Democratic Deficit: The gap between formal democratic institutions and effective popular control over major decisions
Post-Democracy: Crouch's concept of societies maintaining democratic procedures while real power lies with elites and corporations
Hegemonic Bloc: Gramsci's concept of a stable configuration of social forces combining economic power and cultural leadership
Power Elite: Mills' concept of the small interconnected elite of corporate, military, and political leaders
Pluralism: Dahl's theory that political power is dispersed among multiple competing interest groups
Elite Theory: The theoretical position that a small unified elite makes major decisions without democratic accountability
State: Weber's concept of the organization claiming a monopoly of legitimate violence within a territory
Legitimacy: Weber's concept of the belief in the right to rule accepted as valid by those subject to it
Nationalism: The political ideology holding that nations should be self-governing and culturally distinct
Imagined Communities: Anderson's concept that nations are socially constructed communities imagined as limited and sovereign
Print Capitalism: Anderson's concept of how print media created shared language communities enabling national imagination
Populism: A thin ideology dividing society into the pure people versus the corrupt elite
Authoritarianism: A form of government characterized by concentrated power, limited political freedoms, and suppression of opposition
Totalitarianism: An extreme form of authoritarianism seeking total control over all aspects of life
Sociology of Knowledge: The study of how social position shapes what we know and claim to know
Mannheim's Sociology of Knowledge: The argument that all thought except mathematics is perspectival reflecting social position
Standpoint Epistemology: Smith's argument that knowledge is always produced from a particular social standpoint
Reflexive Sociology: Gouldner's concept of sociology turning its analytical tools on itself
Public Sociology: Burawoy's call for sociology engaging public audiences and contributing to democratic debate
Methodological Individualism: The position that social phenomena must be explained by reference to individual actions
Methodological Holism: The position that social wholes have properties irreducible to their individual components
Suicide Rates: Durkheim's famous demonstration that social facts require social (not individual) explanations
Primary Research: Original data collection for a specific research question
Secondary Research: Analysis of data originally collected by others for different purposes
Qualitative Research: Research methods producing non-numerical data (interviews, ethnography, documents)
Quantitative Research: Research methods producing numerical data (surveys, experiments, statistics)
Mixed Methods: Research combining qualitative and quantitative approaches
Ethnography: The method of sustained immersive fieldwork in a social setting
Participant Observation: Research involving simultaneous participation in and observation of a social setting
Going Native: The risk of excessive immersion in fieldwork compromising analytical distance
Grounded Theory: Glaser and Strauss's inductive method building theory from systematic analysis of data
In-depth Interview: A conversational research method allowing respondents to express meanings in their own terms
Focus Group: A group interview method generating data through participant interaction
Content Analysis: The systematic coding and analysis of media or document content
Discount Analysis: The analysis of media representations examining how language constructs social reality
Narrative Analysis: The analysis of stories and storytelling as social phenomena
Survey Research: Research using standardized questionnaires to collect data from populations or samples
Experiment: A research method involving controlled manipulation of variables
Natural Experiment: A situation in which external circumstances create the conditions of an experiment
Case Study: An in-depth analysis of a single case (person, group, organization, event)
Comparative Method: Research comparing cases across societies or historical periods
Triangulation: The use of multiple methods, data sources, or theories to study the same phenomenon
Validity: The degree to which a research measure actually measures what it claims to measure
Reliability: The consistency and replicability of research findings
Generalizability: The extent to which findings from a sample can be applied to broader populations
Ecological Fallacy: Inferring individual-level properties from group-level data
Hawthorne Effect: The tendency for research subjects to change behavior when they know they are being observed
Positivism: The epistemological position that society can and should be studied with the same methods as natural sciences
Interpretivism: The epistemological position that social reality requires methods uncovering subjective meanings
Post-positivism: The position that social inquiry can be rigorous without claiming the same objectivity as natural science
Critical Realism: Bhaskar's position that structures and mechanisms exist independently of our knowledge of them
Ontology: The philosophical study of the nature of existence and being
Epistemology: The philosophical study of the nature and limits of knowledge
Value Freedom: Weber's principle that scientific analysis should be separated from personal value commitments
Reflexivity: The ongoing critical examination of how one's position shapes the research process
Positionality: The recognition that researchers' social location shapes what they can observe and how they interpret
Covert Research: Research in which participants are not aware they are being studied
Informed Consent: Ethical requirement that research participants are fully informed and freely consent to participation
Research Ethics: The principles governing the conduct of research including protection from harm and confidentiality
Representative Sample: A sample reflecting the characteristics of the broader population from which it is drawn
Sampling: The process of selecting a subset of a population for research
Random Sampling: A sampling method giving every member of the population an equal chance of selection
Biographical Method: A qualitative approach collecting and analyzing personal life accounts
Life Course Sociology: The study of how social structures shape lives over time through critical periods and transitions
Cumulative Disadvantage: Dannefer's concept that social inequalities grow more pronounced over the life course
Social Construction of Reality: Berger and Luckmann's concept that social reality is produced through human activity
Externalization: Berger and Luckmann's concept of humans pouring meaning and institutions onto the world
Objectivation: Berger and Luckmann's concept of human products confronting their creators as objective reality
Internalization: Berger and Luckmann's concept of individuals absorbing objective social world as subjective reality
Reification: Berger and Luckmann's concept of treating human-made institutions as natural objects
Phenomenological Sociology: Schutz's application of Husserl's phenomenology to the study of social life
Natural Attitude: Schutz's concept of the taken-for-granted practical orientation of everyday life
Typifications: Schutz's concept of shared interpretive schemes enabling understanding without complete individual knowledge
Intersubjectivity: The sharing of subjective states between individuals making social life possible
Micro-Sociology: The study of small-scale face-to-face social interactions
Macro-Sociology: The study of large-scale social structures, institutions, and historical processes
Micro-Macro Link: The theoretical challenge of connecting individual interactions to larger social structures
Emergence: The property of social phenomena having characteristics not present in their individual components
Sociology of Time: The analysis of how time is socially organized and experienced differently across social positions
Social Imaginary: Taylor's concept of the pre-theoretical understandings making collective practices possible and legitimate
Civil Religion: Bellah's quasi-religious beliefs, symbols, and rituals surrounding the American nation
Collective Memory: Halbwachs's concept that memory is socially constructed and maintained through group frameworks
Cultural Diamond: Griswold's analytical framework connecting cultural object, creator, receiver, and social world
Art Worlds: Becker's concept of artistic production as collective action through networks following conventions
Field of Cultural Production: Bourdieu's concept of the structured space of artistic positions organized by competition
Institutionalization: The process through which social arrangements become established, taken-for-granted, and durable
Path Dependence: The phenomenon in which past decisions constrain future choices creating institutional lock-ins
New Institutionalism: DiMaggio and Powell's theory that organizations adopt similar structures due to institutional pressures
Isomorphism: DiMaggio and Powell's concept of organizations becoming structurally similar through coercive, mimetic, or normative pressures
Functionalist Theory of Stratification: Davis and Moore's argument that inequality motivates talented people to fill important positions
Intersectional Feminism: The approach applying intersectionality theory to feminist analysis and activism
Third Wave Feminism: The feminist movement critiquing second wave's insufficient attention to race, class, and sexuality
Postcolonial Feminism: The feminist framework challenging Eurocentrism and analyzing gendered aspects of colonial legacies
